subtopic: THREATENED STOPPAGE OF WORK AT ARVIDA PLANT OF ALUMINUM COMPANY
speechtext:
My information about
the situation at Ajrvida is that I was advised by the company yesterday that the company had received a telegram from the secretary of the American Federation of Labour affiliate at Arvida to say that unless the company opened negotiations with that union within seventy-two hours the members of the union would be withdrawn from the plant. The company has a sole bargaining agreement with the Catholic Syndicate, a rival union, due to expire at the end of December, 1943. No steps have been taken other than that the government has considered ways and means of maintaining law and order in the event of a walkout.
I saw an unfortunate reference in a Montreal newspaper this morning to the effect that sabotage had occurred in the last strike at Arvida and that the government have taken steps to prevent a similar occurrence this time. It was clearly proved by a commission following the last stoppage of work at Arvida that no sabotage occurred,

and any steps the government are considering now have nothing to do with the situation that occurred before. We are simply considering ways and means of maintaining law and order in case anything does occur.
I iuay say that the aluminum plant is the most important single operation in Canada's munitions programme. There are some eleven thousand employees engaged in manufacturing aluminum. The demand for aluminum for the manufacture of aeroplanes exceeds the supply and will continue to do so for some time. The government therefore feel that they must take unusual precautions to see that no interruption occurs at the aluminum company's plant.
Mr. MacINNlS: Does the minister know whether the Department of Labour has sent an investigator into the area?

I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. I regret that owing to pressure I was not able to get any notice to him. It arises out of a report in the newspapers to-day of a decision in the Exchequer Court by Mr. Justice Thorson to the effect that a soldier is not an officer or servant of the crown within the meaning of section 19(c) of the Exchequer Court Act, and that the crown is not liable for damages caused to persons by negligence on the part of a soldier in the performance of his duties. I am not rising to question in any way the legal decision, but if that is the law I think it is an unfortunate state of affairs. We all know that accidents occui, sometimes through no negligence, sometimes through negligence on the part of one party and sometimes through negligence on the part of another party, and in a clear case of negligence on the part of a member of the armed forces, we will say in the driving of a motor vehicle, as a result of which a citizen loses his life or sustains damage to his property, apparently there is no redress. I suggest to the minister that he ought to reconsider that position and would

REQUEST FOI! STATEMENT ON SHIPPING SITUATION -NORTH AFRICA COMMAND
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of ways and means.

In my absence from the house yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) answered a question I had put about the grave Atlantic peril, and I should like to take a few minutes to mention a matter which affects the safety of every soldier, sailor and air force man who crosses the Atlantic, as well as our shipping, our munitions and our food. These are all in very great danger. According to yesterday's newspapers the last convoy from Canada to England was in very grave danger from submarines, because of the fact that we have not the naval bases that we had during the last war and must use the north and not the south passage to England. Several times last session, when I raised this question, the Prime Minister , promised that he would make a statement in this connection, but he has not done so. I have been raising this question ever since the beginning of the war but nothing has been done. I have in my hand copies of the British Hansard; many members of the British house have been asking similar questions, and there has been debate on many occasions, and recently they were told by Mr. Eden to wait and see. Well, we have waited for over four years but as yet we have not seen. I believe the public should be told the actual facts about this situation. As Mr. Lloyd George said in the British house, if we had not had those bases in the last war we would have lost it. I have had letters from some of my constituents whose sons have been on those ships and who have seen the danger. Some of them have lost their lives, and I have a duty to perform in their behalf.

I referred to this question during the very first days of the present war, after the sinking of the Athenia and the Belvedere off Eire, and I have repeated it at various times. We in this house follow the practice in the British house; our rules are based upon theirs, but we do not get the same results. In this British Hansard there are almost twenty-five pages of questions in regard to the war, but we do not have anything like that here.
That is the first point I want to make. The second question is in connection with the invitation we were given to attend the film, "Desert Victory". I think the Prime Minister should have given this house and the people of Canada a statement in regard to what I call, and what has been called in the British House of Commons, the pro-Vichy policy of Washington. That matter has been debated on several occasions in the British house, and I think some statement on it should have been made here. There was a great deal of criticism in England, and in spite of the popularity of the brilliant Prime Minister and Mr. Eaen, there were objections on the part of many hon. members of the British house to the political policy followed in. North Africa, where our brilliant generals have been supplanted, and all that sort of thing. Darlan was taken out of prison on the arrival of the Americans in North Africa and placed at the head of affairs there, although Vichy was done with. The result was that 700,000 Frenchmen left France, took their belongings and went to North Africa, and wanted Vichy destroyed, and all its treachery. America picked Darlan up and put him in command; and we have had nothing but American politics-not military strategy-in command in Africa. Wait and see.
A statement should be made in this house. One was asked for many times in the British House of Commons. WTe should be told why those brilliant generals of ours w'ere supplanted by someone who never had any experience in battle. Our eighth army, which did all the fighting-Montgomery, Alexander, Wavell, Auchinlech-brilliant military men of all time, were discarded for American politics.
The Prime Minister is not here to-day, and I was not here yesterday. But I say a statement should be given to the house immediately. We have become too Vichy-Washing-ton-minded in our administration of the war.
I believe our United States allies and our other allies will think more of us if criticism were answered here in the House of Commons. Let the people have the facts, rather than take somebody's say-so for it.

It is difficult to give up-to-date figures on the collecting of income tax within various income brackets. The latest figures I have been able to get are for the assessments made in the year 1941-42. I believe I understand the significance of the figures I have. They are given over the signature of Mr. C. F. Elliott and, I say again, they are not the amounts collected in 1941-42, but rather the amounts assessed in that year. Comparing the figures for the amount assessed in that year with the amount assessed in the previous year I find there was a net increase of $4,000,000 in the total amount of income tax assessed. But on breaking that figure down one discovers there was an increase of $11,000,000 collected from those making $10,000 or less, and an actual decrease of $7,000,000 from those above $10,000.
I am well aware that these assessments made in 1941-42 were for the year previous, or possibly for the second year previous, and that changes have been made in the income tax legislation since. But even back in those days it was argued that in order to gather in a large volume of money from income taxation it was necessary to dip into the lower brackets. When the returns are finally tabulated, in whatever years these assessments were for, we discover there was an actual increase of $11,000,000 in respect of those making $10,000 or less, and an actual decrease of $7,000,000 in respect of those making $10,000 or more. When we break down the first figure we find that-

And, if I may repeat, the total assessed in 1940-41 was approximately $51,000,000. The total assessed in 1941-42 was about $55,000,000, making a net increase of about $4,000,000. I am pointing out that this net increase of $4,000,000 divides itself into two groups. There is a net increase of S11,000,000 in the brackets up to $10,000 and a net decrease of $7,000,000 in the brackets over $10,000.
Mr. ILSLEYr:	That means that a great
many more persons in the lower brackets were employed, does it not?

I should be glad if the
minister would give further information to explain that situation. I might explain in fairness to the figures that they might be for the year 1939-40 or for the year 1940-41. The increase of $11,000,000 in the brackets up to $10,000 would seem to bear heavily on the lower brackets in that section. In connection with those in the brackets up to $2,000 there is a net increase of $3,500,000. In other words, $3,500,000 out of the $11,000,000 increase I referred to as applying to those up to $10,000 was taken from those earning $2,000 or less. What I am anxious to point out by giving these figures is the fact that back in those days it was being argued that in order to collect a sufficiently large volume of money the treasury had to dip into the lower brackets as low as it did. But the figures which have been compiled a year or two later are ominous in that they indicate that there was an increase in what was taken from those in the lower brackets while there was a decrease in what was taken from those in the higher brackets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What is ominous about
them? What do they show except that there has been an increase in the national income in the lower brackets rather than in the higher brackets? What do they show except that a greater number of persons in the brackets up to $2,000 were working or were earning a higher wage or more wages? Perhaps they were not earning a higher hourly wage, but they were earning more wages. It might also

indicate that the rates of wages were increased. In fact, they were increased in 1940 and again in 1941.
I do not understand the deduction the hon. gentleman draws. Is he suggesting that more could have been obtained from those in the higher income brackets? There was an actual reduction in the tax assessed but there certainly was no reduction in the rates. Those rates were increased much more than the rates in the lower brackets. Even at that they produced a lower return. This simply proves what I have been stating, that the great increase in the national income has gone to the persons in the lower income brackets.

I am not objecting to
the increases in taxation taken from those in the lower brackets, but I am perplexed by the fact that while there was this increase, there was a decrease in the tax assessed against those in the upper brackets. The minister suggests that a larger total volume of income was being received by those in the lower brackets. Was there not also a larger total volume being received by those in the higher brackets?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think there was.
I must say I should have thought that the higher rates imposed against those in the upper brackets would have more than offset any decrease in income received.

I shall be glad to send a copy of these figures over to the minister. They came from the income tax division. I should appreciate it if he would look into them and make some explanation as to why they worked out in this way. My feeling is that the dipping has gone too low. I should have hoped that these resolutions 9 and 10 would go farther than they do with regard to consideration for those in the lower brackets. Instead of giving this slight incentive to people to earn more than $660 or $1,200 as the case may be, there could have been a raising of that minimum figure. One hesitates to suggest a compromise when he is making his principal request, but I suggest that if the exemption level cannot be raised the minister give consideration to making a larger portion of the tax paid by those in the lower brackets compulsory savings. Perhaps all of it might be considered as compulsory savings. That would not interfere with the minister's endeavour to cut down purchasing power and prevent inflation. Money would be brought into the treasury but in the long run there would not be such a heavy burden placed upon those in the lower brackets. My suggestion is that instead of resolutions 9 and 10

making the provisions that they do up to a certain figure there should be a raising of the lower exemption level, or a provision that the entire amount of income tax paid by those in certain brackets should be considered as compulsory savings.
Is the hon. member reading from a factual statement by the commissioner of income tax, or is he giving his own interpretation of figures which have been placed before him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes.

I would ask the minister to
give consideration to the position of the piece worker and the reduced effort which is caused by the present income tax on increased earnings of piece workers. The minister and his department might give some consideration to the desirability of restoring the incentive which has always prompted the piece worker, who, perhaps by exceptional skill, more often because of exceptional strength, can work long hours and contribute in a very important degree to a greater war effort, but who to-day, finding himself taxed so heavily on his increased earnings, because of the higher scale applicable to his additional earnings obtained over more than the normal hours, finds no incentive to continue this increased effort.
I realize the minister's problem, and 1 recognize the necessity of taxation, but it seems to me that some incentive should be left.
W7hen we have a situation in which a man possessed of exceptional skill or strength can make $5 in a normal day, but by greater effort and longer hours can make from seven to nine dollars a day, but has practically no more net earnings when his pay is $7.50 than when it is $5 or $5.50, the incentive disappears. Some provision should be made to restore the incentive to the piece worker who is giving war service, whether in a munitions plant, in the bush, or elsewhere. The lack of it is felt in the industrial plants, and also definitely in bush work, all across the dominion. We have had appeals for greater effort to compensate for the shortage of men engaged in lumbering. Yet many men to-day are quitting at mid-day, or not later than the middle of the afternoon, although capable of continuing and producing almost double their present output; they say, "Well, we have worked this long for ourselves; we are not going to work the rest of the day for the government." Surely amendments
Income War Tax

could be made which would so distribute the tax rates as to leave these men some incentive to exert themselves more fully. I realize that the problem is a difficult one, but with careful, indeed scientific consideration, the tax schedules could be so adjusted as to leave the man with greater earning power an incentive, not only to earn $10 by hard toil, but to give us $10 worth of real war effort. I think the minister realizes the need as well as the possibilities of such an amendment. He knows that the present system is seriously affecting production in many districts, and promises to affect it similarly in the coming year. I do not suggest it should be remedied by penalizing the man who normally earns around $2 or $2.50. But in most cases these men have their choice to work either by the month or by the piece, and if they feel they are capable enough and strong enough to put in long hours and give us the production in different lines of industry, the incentive should not be lacking, particularly since we are so short of men and the employment situation promises to be critical.

I wish to cite an example of what seems to me an unfair situation in connection with the income tax regulations.
I mentioned something of the same kind a year ago.
An elderly widow who was living in a house of substantial size, and whose family had grown up and established themselves in their own homes, found it necessary, owing to the impossibility of carrying on, to sell her home. She had, I believe, an income of about $2,500. The house was clear of encumbrance, excepting a mortgage of $2,000. Her total expenses, including interest on mortgage, municipal tax, telephone, water, light, janitor, maid, fuel, repairs to the house and other incidentals, but not including food, came to about $1,798. She would have to pay $500 income tax on an income of $2,500, which would reduce her net income to approximately $2,000; and deducting $1,798, made up of the items I have mentioned, would leave her $202. Adding the $660 she is allowed as a single woman gave her $862 upon which to live, provide food, and maintain an elderly widowed sister. It meant that she would have $2.36 a day, with the strain of carrying on; therefore she sold her house. That is one example, I have not the slightest doubt, of the position of scores and scores of widowed people. I mentioned it to the minister last year, but he did not see his way clear to make provision for such cases. This woman ranks as a single person, and perhaps in the eyes of the income tax department is properly so classified, but, faced with the necessity of carrying on a large house with a maid, a janitor, and all these other expenses, it does 
not seem to be fair that she should be forced to sell her home and go to live with somebody else, perhaps, or in a room; for obviously she could not live in a large house and maintain herself on $860 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Dufferin-Simcoe raised the question of piece workers. It is a very difficult problem, as he understands. I cannot give any solution. The matter is being studied by the Department of National Revenue to see if anything can be done so that these workmen will not feel that there is no incentive to work. I am afraid I cannot add much to that. It relates to the problem of absenteeism raised by the hon. member for Danforth. It is absenteeism caused by the progressive element in the taxation. I do not know just how much there is of that, but there is undoubtedly some.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is quite a progressive element in the taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To change the tax so that
the person who earns more is taxed no more would be a retrograde step.' As the hon. member said himself, it is pretty hard to argue that a person earning $2 a day should be taxed at the same rate as one earning $10.
Is absenteeism widespread ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Opinions differ about that.
I think there is undoubtedly some as the result of income taxation. I think there is more due to other causes. Income taxation is not the sole cause, I should say not the main cause. That is shown by the absenteeism that we read about in the United States where they do not have this progressive taxation on workmen-that is by way of deduction.

Many people
speak loosely about it, but has the minister any actual figures as to absenteeism in Canada ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know what the
figures are.

I think
the minister will agree that there is a good deal of absenteeism, especially in the munitions plants. This year as we went about, one of the things brought to our attention was the extent to which there was absenteeism.
If resolution 10 was intended or partly intended to do away with absenteeism to a certain extent, it will not meet the requirement. Could there be some sort of system of production exemption? If a man reaches his maximum, of say $1,250 and if the production of the plant had increased, might not

Income War Tax
a portion of the increase be allowed him tax free, thereby encouraging him to work say another day or half day to increase the production, and so that all of that increase would not be taken away from him?
The problem is a serious one. Industrialists pointed out to us on a number of occasions that a large number of men are staying home after reaching the limit of their tax free amount. They would not work any more, because if they did they were only working for the government. If some adjustment could be made in that regard it would help our war effort.

I gather from conversations I have had with workers and managers that there is a good deal of ground for believing that the comment of the hon. member for Danforth the other night that probably ten per cent of the workers take advantage of the situation as regards income tax is correct. The difficulty seems to be that the workman sees his income tax deduction in relation to his weekly earnings. He feels that because he has earned a certain amount this week and has paid a part of that in taxes he was working for the government. The point the workman does not see is that his income tax is levied on the entire year's earnings, and that if he does not multiply this week's earnings by fifty-two there will probably be something coming to him on the income tax. This suggestion has been made by employers that the department prepare a leaflet or pamphlet for distribution to workers pointing out that their income tax is levied over the entire year and that if for a part of that year they are paying more than their year's income would warrant they will probably have a rebate of the overpayment coming to them at the end of the year. They could then see that income tax in relation to their year's earnings, and not in relation to a particular week's earnings. Employers agree that that would help the situation.

Yesterday at
11.30 a group of workmen came to see me on this very matter. This particular group found that one individual *who worked five and a half days in the week was taxed 91 cents a day, whereas others w'ho laid off work on Monday and worked only four and a half days in the week paid a per diem tax of only 30 cents. The full force of taxation on the average workmen's wages comes out of the sixth day's work. If one lays off that day he finds his taxation so much less. It is true he gets so much less in his pay envelope for the week, but many employees
have chores to do around the house, or they have gardens, or they just want a little leisure.
The answer given as to what obtains in the United States does not cover the whole case. In the United States they have an overall tax, a victory tax of five per cent.
With regard to the answer given by the Minister of National Revenue that they have a right to file a claim for refund if they have paid too much on their total year's earnings, that does not help much, because I venture to say as high as fifty per cent of the industrial workers will not make application for any return. They are not properly advised by employers, to begin with; they are not properly advised by the department itself. I am in accord with the hon. member for York South when he says they ought to be properly advised. Another point is that they often change employers during the year, causing difficulty so far as the yearly' return is concerned.
I urge that consideration be given to ways and means of reducing the taxation on the employee who works six or five and a half days a week and so earns an amount just over that which makes him taxable. If that condition could be dealt with by departmental regulations I am satisfied that the honest workman would feel a good deal better about it alongside of the man who absents himself and does not do a full week's work.

This is a big problem, not only in Canada but also in the United States, and in Britain, where I discussed it with Sir Kingsley Wood in September, 1941. For the first time in history a large group of people, mechanics and workmen of all kinds, were being called upon to pay income tax, and the government authorities over there were shocked and startled to learn that a goodly number of people stopped work when they reached what they considered to be the limit at which they would begin to pay taxes. It is a problem. I think there will have to be some morale building; an appeal must be made to them to continue production. In the companies where pulpwood is cut under contract I am told that these men stop work -some of them stop work; not all, I am glad to think-when they have produced a certain amount, and they have two or three hours of leisure. Of course that is very hard work; I would not like to be dogmatic and say that they stop because they do not want to earn any more, but in any case many of them do stop after having worked about seven or eight hours. What the country needs, I think, is
Income War Tax

some sort of appeal to the morale of these people, that they should go on producing and contributing, because every man has a stake in this country; every man has his part to play, and they, as producers of raw materials, have their place in the picture. It is their war, too. I often wonder if an appeal could not be made direct to these men by their employers- I do not know who else could do it-to keep on working even if they have to pay some taxation. My own view is that this problem will have to be dealt with sooner or later, especially if the government should ever contemplate increasing the taxes.	.
I find, too, that there is considerable resentment at the theory of deduction at the source. The men see this and that taken off their pay, and they look only at the residue. I saw the stub of a company cheque that went out, showing I think six deductions from the man's cheque, though of course some of those were deductions he had asked to have made. Just what the minister is going to do about it I do not know, but since we were told yesterday by the minister that seventy-five per cent of the increase in the national income goes to the lower wage earning groups, I do not think anyone should advocate that they be relieved altogether from the payment of income tax. That is where I think we will have to get a large share of the money. Make them have a sense of national obligation, if you can, by a morale building crusade; that they are part of this great national effort. That is the only suggestion I can offer to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I should like to say something about the suggestion offered by the hon. member for Danforth, because I think there is a great deal of merit in it. The problem has been that where two men are engaged at the same rate, one man may work, six days a week and the other man only four days. If the pay period is either one week or two weeks, when the employer is working out the tax to be deducted from the wages of these men he takes as his basis the amount the man is paid during that period. If one man has been away for two or three days in the period his wage is less and his deductions are made at a very much lower rate. I take it that what the hon. member for Danforth suggests is that in these cases a man on a daily rate of pay should have the deductions made on that daily rate, whether he works only one day in a week or two days in two weeks; that the deductions be made at the daily rate the man is paid, as though he had been working every day in the week.

I am very anxious that the minister shall not put into my mouth words which I never used. The impression that may be left by the observations the minister is now making is that in many industries they find it impossible to provide sufficient work to keep their employees going for a full six days, with the result that they work only perhaps four days, in which case the employee on a daily basis finds himself without enough pay in his envelope to look after his family. That is not what was in my mind at all. We must not in any circumstances allow taxation to reach into any pay envelope which does not contain sufficient to support a man's family at a fairly decent level. That is basic. But those who have regular and steady employment but who absent themselves from that employment, thus disrupting the production of that organization, should have their tax equalized. At the same time those in the same organization who patriotically work full time, and overtime when they can, in order to increase production, should have some incentive which would encourage them to keep on doing so. In view of the fact that recent press reports have suggested that some of us in this chamber were anxious to tax those in the lower brackets, I am anxious to make the point clear as far as the people of Canada are concerned, and at the same time I should like to see some method found which would.encourage those who are anxious to produce

Before this matter is dismissed by the minister I suggest that he confer with those in industry who are familiar with this problem. There is a tremendous shortage of highly specialized, efficient men who can do a particular job in certain industries. Those men are being pressed to work long hours, for the very reason that there is'a shortage of highly trained men in these particular branches. These men work extra hours; there is no question about that, but they are penalized in regard to the payment of income tax, and week by week they are told by the other men, "Well, you did a patriotic job but you are not getting much consideration for it." I have spoken to men in that position, men who have worked until they were ready to drop just because they were needed on a special operation. I submit to the minister, following what has been said by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simeoe and the hon. member for Danforth, that most serious consideration should be given to men of this kind, because there are not enough of them. They do very important work, and their earnest desire to help is more or less

Income War Tax
ridiculed by the other workmen. As a result their determination is being undermined, until they reach the point where they say, "Well, why should I continue to be the victim of these circumstances, when I aim supposed to be needed so urgently?" I would ask the minister to confer with others on this point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I should not like the impression to go abroad for a moment that we are dismissing the suggestions that have been offered; not at all. As I see it, the way it would work out is this. A man engaged at a daily rate would have deductions made at that daily rate, so that if he stayed away from work for two or three days he would still have deductions made from his daily pay equal to the amount that would have been deducted per day if he had worked all week. In the end that would mean a refund coming to that man, but in the meantime he would have' the same amount deducted per day as from the man who worked a full week. With regard to the other class mentioned by the hon. member for Danforth, namely people who have intermittent work, we have already had to deal with them. There are some classes- and I might mention longshoremen particularly-who have work for two or three days a week, and who may be then laid off two or three days. Consequently special arrangements have had to be made to average out their receipts, so that deductions may be made which are not at the daily rate for the few days worked, when it is known they are not going to be working for the remainder of the week. Those cases have been dealt with specially.

I do not wish to press the question or take up too much of the time of the committee, but I feel that we have offered criticism without suggesting much in the way of a solution. I cannot help thinking that some consideration must be given to the question as to what constitutes an average day. If the over-all receipts of taxes from piece workers were reduced, even if it involved a smaller collection of taxes, and an addition made to taxes on incomes in the higher brackets, or even to corporation taxes, it does seem to me it would have a far-reaching effect. Some have said this afternoon that they doubt how effective this could be. I know from personal knowledge that in many instances there has been a decrease of from twenty-five per cent to thirty per cent in production. That means a tremendous volume. I know of one instance where men have actually reduced their output by almost half. It has been shown that by producing a certain amount men can have just as much as by having greater production. It does seem to me that in respect of piece
workers we shall have to impose a tax that is no higher on the fifth unit than on the third. There is certainly much merit in what was said by the hon. members for Lincoln and Danforth. I believe it is shown from what has been said by the hon. member for Danforth that those in the low brackets should not have to pay this tax, nor that those who had only four or five days work in a week should suffer. But when a man is taxed low on one unit of production, and then a little higher on the next, and reaches the point where on his fifth unit of production his rate of taxation is excessively high, he comes to the conclusion that he has just as much money by producing only three or four units. I have had personal experience in cases where production has dropped down by almost fifty per cent. I am certain the same situation will exist next year, and I do urge upon the minister and his department that they give further consideration to the matter so that during the coming months he may be able to maintain the production which is now so essential. I am sure something can be done, even at the risk of sacrificing some of the total taxation from piece workers; it can be added somewhere else. Our war effort demands that we do this; otherwise we are not going to get full benefit of the services of efficient piece workers.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: These two sections are designed for the purpose of curing the situation about which the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has spoken. If a married man had an income .of about $1,200 or less a year he would not be taxable. But if he increased his production and came into the taxable class the amount of his tax would reduce his income to the exempted amount. Consequently the additional amount he would be earning would be taken away in taxation. To avoid that, these sections have been introduced, so that any increased earning above the exemption level of $660 and $1,200 may be distributed, one-third to the man himself, one-third in refundable savings and the other one-third as tax. That is the situation covered by these two sections.
That is up to $820 is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That condition would not arise with incomes above $820 or $1,570.

The problem we have in Canada was met in England. Over there at the end of the quarter they established an annual earning rate for the individual based on his total earnings for the previous quarter. During the next quarter they would say: You earned at such-and-such an annual rate during the last quarter, and we are taxing you

Income War Tax

during the present quarter at such a rate, in equal amounts each week, based on your previous earnings. The result was that the worker knew what his tax was going to be each week. There was every incentive for him to work the extra hours, because he knew he would get the benefit of those extra hours' work at the rate of time-and-a-half or time-and-a-quarter overtime. He knew his deduction for purposes of taxation would be a certain fixed number of shillings on his weekly payroll, and that anything over and above that amount would be his.
There are advantages ini this system. I happened to be in England, in the vicinity of some of the coal mines during one of the most critical periods of the war, when there was a desperate need for fuel production. Management, trade unions, government-all were urging the miners to work seven days a week. In several of the collieries I visited they were working at that rate. They were receiving time and a half for the Sunday work-and I say that subject to correction, because it may have been time and a third. Anyway they were drawing large weekly payrolls.
Under our system we would say to those miners: You are earning so much at this very much increased annual rate. We would then deduct that amount from the weekly wages. The deduction would be heavy. The English system has the effect of equalizing those extra hours of work over a quarterly period, and results in encouraging the men to work extra hours. It has greatly reduced absenteeism and the desire to chuck it on a Saturday afternoon and go to the races or to a football match. The man knows that if this week he works an extra number of hours his payroll will be increased by that extra amount of cash, and that is a great incentive. Although I do not speak with absolute accuracy, I believe the supply of coal increased during the extra drive by as much as eighteen or twenty per cent. I commend that statement to the Minister because I have seen this system work satisfactorily in England.

I agree with the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) when he says that there has been much loose talk during the past two years about absenteeism. So far I have seen no proof that there is actually a great deal of absenteeism, and I doubt if there are many men staying away from work because of income tax. There are many factors that enter into this matter which must be understood. First, the people of this country have been taught over a long period of time to live on one or two days' work per 
week; we compelled them to live on that. You cannot take people who have never worked, who have been obliged to sleep most of their time, and put them at heavy work and expect them to work seven days a week. It is not possible physically.
Then again older men are being employed. How many men in this house could work 365 days in the year without taking a day off? Many people are obliged to stay home because of the physical impossibility of continuing at work six or seven days a week. Many industries in Canada had adopted a five-day week and the workers had become used to it. Much of the work being done by men and women in factories across the country is of a type which necessitates their taking a day off occasionally. A lot of men are losing time because of a shortage of machinery or because of breakages. I know that some employers are in the habit of classifying these lay-offs as absenteeism. That is not a fair classification.
One thing that would help to keep people on the job continuously is a system of vacations with pay. When a man is working 365 days a year without anything in the way of vacation to look forward to he is bound to take off a day occasionally. It may not be possible to put in effect a system of vacations with pay while we are fighting this war, but I think that will have to come.
Some of the regional boards are requiring that now.

I am glad to hear that. There has been a good deal of exaggeration in connection with absenteeism. I am informed that the Canadian Car and Foundry company, Montreal, recently had a survey made by medical authorities. Some practical work was done in connection with lost time in the different plants and it was finally cut down fifty per cent. The experiments carried on were one hundred per cent successful. I believe it was Doctor Finney who carried on these experiments. When he tried to interest other industries in this matter he was given the brush-off; they were not interested.
I have been corresponding with the minister of pensions with regard to this matter and I believe he is now making an investigation. I think the hon. member for Danforth was very fair in his statement that only a small percentage of the men employed are resentful at the deductions being made and are taking a day off in order to avoid placing themselves in the higher income classification. The percentage is actually very small, and many statements in this regard have been exaggerated.
While there has been no increase this year in the income tax rates, the average man in industry does not understand the set-up. It

Income War Tax
was expected that there would be no increase in the deductions, but actually the deductions have been stepped up quite substantially. This comes as a surprise to them, and the salaried workers and others across the country will be hit hard at the end of June, when they make their returns, and in December. The matter has been settled and nothing can be done about it, but there will be considerable resentment until these people get back on an even keel. I realize that we cannot fight a war without taxation, but an effort should be made to explain these things to the people. If we are in earnest about fighting the war, we must pay for it. There will be no pie in the sky while we are fighting the war. This lack of information and the creating of a wrong impression has been responsible for much of the criticism that has been offered.
I have received many telegrams on this matter and I have advised the people that there is no way we can get from under except to carry, on an agitation for more equal sacrifices during the process of fighting this war. To stand up in the house or outside the house and make the flatfooted statement that production is being curtailed because of absenteeism is creating a wrong impression. Very few men and women are staying home because of the income tax or because they do not want to do their proportionate share in promoting our war effort. The physical factor is the important one. Men and women find that they must take a day off from time to time, they just cannot stand up to it.

Would the minister reply to the suggestion I have made? I suggested first that the levels of $660 and $1,200 might be raised, but I take it that that is out this year so far as he is concerned. My alternative suggestion was that consideration should be given to persons earning between $660 and $820, in the one case, and between $1,200 and $1,570, in the other, and provide that a larger portion than fifty per cent, as now provided, be regarded as compulsory savings to be returned to the taxpayer after the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The matter of the proportion to be returnable was given exhaustive study before it was introduced into the budget last year. I do not think from what I hear that the returning of a larger part would be regarded by a wage-earner or taxpayers generally as a greater incentive to work. They are more concerned about the deduction than they are about the part that is to be returned to them. That is one of the difficulties. You hear a great many of them say: We do not know when we will get this back. Some even say: AVe do not know whether we will get
72537-134J
this back. We have to reiterate the truth, which is that they will get back that part which is being deducted as compulsory savings. In that respect employers could assist a great deal, and I think do assist a great deal, by explaining that part of the deduction is savings. The gradations of the portion of the tax which is savings have been very carefully and very justly worked out, and I would not care to alter that. It starts at 50 per cent for the lower incomes and works out to a very small percentage for the high incomes. It is not easy to alter these relationships. They would have to be altered all along the line and in such a way that the alterations would bear a just relationship to one another.
They are dependent upon mathematical calculations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. I do not think that the bon. member's suggestion would be effective as a means of providing a greater immediate incentive.
I .am very much impressed by the suggestion of the hon. member for York West about taking a quarterly period and making a flat deduction from the payroll of the next period on the basis of the earnings of the previous period. He says that the results in the English experience have been favourable. It might be possible to go a considerable distance towardls .doing that here. It could not be done in some industries, I assume, but it might be done in many, and it might be the best way of overcoming this difficulty. I am informed that it could be done by order in council, that it does not require legislation.
May I ask when the minister expects to have ready the certificates evidencing the returnable portion of the tax?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
The portion of the. tax that is compulsory savings can be determined only when the income, tax return has finally been filed, because, the deductions that are now being made at the source are only approximations. Last year they were based on 90 per cent of the tax due, and this year 95 per cent, but the actual amount of compulsory savings will be known for each individual taxpayer only when the income tax return is filed. On the taxpayer's receipt will be shown the amount of compulsory savings standing to his credit. The question has been under consideration whether a special certificate should also be given showing the amount of compulsory savings standing to the credit of the taxpayer, but no decision has yet been reached on that point.
Income War Tax
That applies only to .personal income tax, but corporations have also paid in compulsory savings and carry it as an asset on their balance sheet.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
The income tax receipt
shows the amount standing to their credit.

Yesterday there seemed to be some confusion in the mind of the Minister of Finance in regard to the matter of which I spoke the day before yesterday and again yesterday, and the hon. member for Parry Sound made the same suggestion, namely, that in that class of taxpayer, mostly in the junior professional class and the undermanagerial class who receive over $2,500 up to let us say $6,000-1 am speaking only of that class, not of any others-the differentiation between the exemption given to a married man with no children and receiving, let us say, $4,000, and the exemption given to a married man with four children and receiving $4,000 was inadequate, in the sense that it did not recognize any responsibility- not the whole responsibility-of keeping the children or providing for the total expenses incidental to their upkeep.
I merely wish to point out to the minister that certainly I for my part was not advocating any change! affecting those getting $2,500 or less who benefit through the change in the method of granting exemptions. My argument, the minister will see if he reads it, was confined solely to the married man without children and getting $4,000 or upwards and the married man with two or three or four children and coming within the same brackets. I think the budget when it was brought down last year containing this change was regarded across the country as a budget which worked against the family, and this is one of the repercussions of the change which was made at that time. I have asked the minister to give some consideration to the information which I have brought before the house and which was contained in a brief sent to me from a lawyers' firm in Toronto. The minister took the attitude that attack was the best defence and suggested that on this point I was speaking for a certain class of people whom I did not care to be associated with exclusively. Let me say to him that I have no hesitation in standing up here for the enterprise system in which I believe. The class of people for whom I was speaking, particularly those in the junior professional class, are represented by the letterhead of the firm which sent me the brief. There are altogether nine partners in this firm. There is an asterisk against the

name of each partner serving overseas, and there are five such. Of the other four members of this firm, to my own personal knowledge three were veterans of the last war. I am proud to stand up for the rights of such people.

Apropos of what the hon. member for Rosedale has just suggested, I would point out that for a man with an income of $3,000 the difference between the tax expense for a single man and a married man with no children is $240; the difference in tax expense between the married man with no children and the married man with one child is $138; the difference in tax expense between the married man with one child and the married man with two children is $112.20; and the difference in tax expense between the married man with two children and the married man with three children is $54. It had to be done; it was a fair thing to do. They could not be expected to invest in property which might become worthless in two or three years, unless they were allowed a rapid write-off. Ordinary depreciation is simply based on that principle, that the property depreciates over a period of years and a write-off is allowed so that the capital will be there; it will be in the hands of the investor at the end of the write-off period. Therefore that, I think, would be a satisfactory enough condition. But there is a way; if these companies are able to sell these properties at the end of the time for a. substantial amount; if, say 100 per cent were written off and they sold it for fifty per cent to themselves or an affiliated or associated company and then began to write it off again, I think it would be said that the country had been generous to them. May I ask just why equipment or machinery is not included in the application of this resolution?
. Mr. ILSLEY: For one thing it is almost impossible to follow equipment and machinery. In the second place a three-year writeoff is not bad for equipment and machinery, especially if they are working on twenty-four hour shifts. The ordinary depreciation rate for machinery is ten per cent, I think, which assumes a ten-year life for a machine; but under present conditions maintenance is not so easy, and when twenty-four hour shifts are worked the life of a machine is probably reduced by more than two-thirds. So that in

the inquiries I was able to make it was not felt that a three-year write-off -was much out of line. The commissioner points out that it is not always three years; it is sometimes four years or five years, or there may be some cases of two years. But in regard to equipment and machinery there is more justification for a rapid write-off, from the point of view of the machinery wearing out during that time, than there is in regard to immovable assets. Altogether apart from that, however, which perhaps is not the main consideration, there would be cases where machinery would1 be worth something at the end of the period. In addition, as I said earlier, it would be very hard to follow machinery or equipment. If a machine is sold to someone it would be difficult to find out the value and allot it to the depreciation which had been allowed on that machinery over the period during which it would be depreciated. It would mean reopening a number of assessments and probably reopening them repeatedly. Accordingly, we thought we should not try to cover equipment and machinery.
I would point out that it might very well be that some persons who entered into agreements with the crown for rapid depreciation had the vague idea in the back of their minds that there might be this capital gain in sight, and for that reason they took the risk of a capital loss. We are not doing anything for them if they sustain a capital loss, but we are distributing the capital gain in the immovable assets back over the life of those immovable assets. There is ground for argument that this is not the proper way to treat them, but after giving the matter a great deal of consideration we thought it was just enough, because the period during which they have been enabled to enjoy war business has been substantial and there will have been few, if any, capital losses. We thought, therefore, it was all right to take the capital gains on these and use them for reduction of the depreciation.

I can see the common sense which has animated the minister in dealing with equipment and machinery. This is somewhat of a new principle, and I suspect its working out will give the department considerable trouble. It may well be that experience will show that perhaps they are not wise principles to assert. Nevertheless, like the hon. member for Bow River, I feel that in war time people who are being asked to contribute to the war effort would feel a sense of frustration if some protection against undue profits, through depreciation, were not accorded by the government. He can offset against this, three types of expenses only-the payment of principal on a mortgage which was in effect or registered prior to June 23, 1942; payments into pension funds-this is not a pension fund -and life insurance premiums. This man does not qualify. It is not life insurance; it is not a payment into a pension fund; it is not a payment on a mortgage. He does not qualify any more than if he had bought a victory bond or any kind of bond. I see no ground on which he could qualify. He is simply making an investment. He is doing it for patriotic purposes, but it is not a savings commitment.

He is in a similar position to those who use their savings for the purpose of paying life insurance premiums. One is just as much a saving as the other.
Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The test is not whether it is savings or not. The test is whether it is savings paid in pursuance of a savings commitment. We would never have made this concession except that in certain cases the failure to keep up certain payments would result in substantial loss or forfeiture. Otherwise we would be led into any worth while or worthy investment, and we would be in a very broad field. We do not allow payments for war savings certificates or victory bonds. Nor is there any ground for allowing expenditures on a non-interest bearing bond as an offset against the refundable portion of the tax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am not sure that this item is the appropriate one on which to ask this question, but I can see no other to which it is more appropriate. My question has to do with the refundable portion of the income tax. In his budget speech the minister made reference to some type of certificate that would be issued to show the refundable portion of the tax standing to the taxpayer's credit. First, may I ask, when does the government expect to commence issuing these certificates, and in what denominations, or how will they be issued?
The minister has answered that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am sorry. Then may I ask this question? When the certificates are issued will they be transferable or negotiable in any way, or will it be stated on the face of the certificates that they are not transferable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The form is not settled. They will be issued after the return for the year is made and the assessment completed, which will be some time after June 30 of this year. They will not be transferable.

The question of issuing bonds is out, I suppose? There was some suggestion at one time, I do not recall just when, that in certain instances bonds would be issued by the treasury to cover the refundable portion. I understand that is out and that to-day the position is that the taxpayer is to get some sort of acknowledgment in writing, what I would call evidence of indebtedness, in some form which has not yet been determined.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

I have here a copy of a letter that was sent to the Minister of Finance. Since it is very important, perhaps the minister would comment upon it. The writer of this letter refers to a

pamphlet "Your 1942 Income Tax", which was issued by the income tax division, and referring to one paragraph in the pamphlet he says:
This paragraph indicates that in respect of a policy on the life of a taxpayer, his wife or a dependent, the amount of the premium may be deducted from the "savings" portion of the 1942 income tax payable. Might this not be extended to cover premiums paid by the taxpayer on behalf of soldiers?
The following situation brought this thought to me: My son, Pte. G. L. Mason, aged 26, and now in England, earned as much as $2,000 per annum before enlisting and has policies amounting to $7,000. All but $2,000 is 20-payment life and of it $5,000 has been current for 10 years or more.
Even were it possible for him to meet the very moderate premiums, amounting to $148.71 per annum, it may well be that in the present circumstances he does not have the inclination to do so. In our case I am at present able and have undertaken to meet these premiums, but is it not reasonable to expect that in not a few similar cases insurance will lapse either through financial inability or through loss of interest by the insured in life insurance?
I rather feel that the maintenance of life insurance, in cases such as that outlined, may be as desirable as the accumulation of savings through the medium of income tax payments. Therefore, I take the liberty of placing these thoughts before you for what they may be worth.
The writer's son. is a private overseas and certainly would not have enough money left out of his $1.30 a day to pay these premiums. If the soldier's father pays the premiums, could he not be allowed to offset them against the compulsory savings portion of the tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not authorized by the act.

But could it not be done? Would it not be fair to do it? There would not be many such cases, and I think in fairness to the soldier- this particular soldier has been making payments on his policies for ten years-that should be allowed as a deduction by the father if he makes the payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is wrong about soldiers not being able to pay their insurance premiums. The lapse record is lower for soldiers than for the civilian population.
Who is paying the premiums?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are paying them.
Not out of their SI .30; somebody else must be paying it. We have no Sparkman act in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The rate is not $1.30 for most of them; it is $1.50.

Income War Tax

That is quite a debatable question. When we come to the war appropriation bill I should like to ask some questions about that, because I am getting a number of letters from men who are not being paid the higher rate. I think the base rate is $1.30, and you cannot pay insurance premiums out of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The base rate, yes.

I should like to support the hon. member for Peterborough West in his suggestion, and, if it can be worked out as an amendment to the provision in the act,
I believe the two ministers should give their assent thereto. There was an article in the Globe and Mail entitled:
Why Young Husbands Lie Awake at Night.
It reads:
It is expected that in the next few months there will be called into the Canadian army young married men of the twenty-five to thirty-year class, and we are acquainted with case histories of a few of them which must be typical of many thousands throughout the country. Their lot is hard; and as some of them view it, they are near despair, not for themselves, but for their families.
I am not suggesting at this particular time anything about the pay in the army. In some cases some people may be able to scrape along on it; but, as the minister well knows, there are some who were married and who had insurance policies and perhaps were in receipt of incomes considerably higher than the total pay and allowances in the army, and they are experiencing a most difficult time. If some parent or relation will maintain the premiums on the soldiers' policy, and it can be made an amendment to the section in the act so that it is not too embracive of extraneous matters, I think the minister should give every consideration to it.
The leader of the opposition mentioned to the minister a change in the section which is under review, namely, allowing a husband to take credit for the payment of principal on a mortgage when the property is held in the wife's name. I do not recall whether, when this section was first put through, last year, the possibility was envisaged. Perhaps it was, but certainly very shortly afterwards I wrote to the Minister of Finance a letter pointing out the extreme hardship I was finding in my riding in connection with many men who had their houses in their wives' names and were now unable to offset the principal payment on the mortgage against their refundable or compulsory savings. The minister wrote me at some length stating that the crown could
not connive, or even lay itself open to a suspicion of conniving, at what might in some instances be a defrauding of creditors, namely, when a husband puts property in a wife's name in order to get away from creditors. Now, as we know, the percentage of husbands who put property in their wives' names for that purpose immediately before going into bankruptcy is infinitesimal, so small that one cannot give cognizance to it; and also, the bankruptcy act in most provinces, or possibly in the dominion, does not allow a transfer to be made within a certain time of bankruptcy taking place. So that the situation has arisen, and I think all hon. members will agree it is a most salutary one, of a husband and father wishing first of all to keep a roof over the head of his family, and to that end he keeps the house where the family live in the wife's name against the possibility of a lawsuit or a commercial disaster. We found there were a great many taxpayers who were in a position of not being able to take credit for the payment of mortgage principal as an offset against their refundable savings. Undoubtedly, as the leader of the opposition has said, this has caused a hardship in many cases where hardship was sought to be averted, namely, by the change in the legal ownership of the property from the wife to the husband, at great expense. I must confess I was much amused when the minister suggested in his letter to me this was the procedure which could be taken and would be recognized. It certainly smacked of a tax avoidance, if not tax evasion, when the Minister of Finance said that one could put a piece of property in his wife's name and thus avoid taxes. However, that only leads me to say that if the minister would accept the suggestions frequently put forward, I hope constructively, from this side of the house and elsewhere, the people of Canada would be better served. In my reading the other day I came across a quotation which, I think, is well worth putting on record for the consideration of the Minister of Finance. It is as follows:
"The value of the political heads of departments", wrote a nineteenth century chancellor of the exchequer, "is to tell the permanent officials what the public will not stand."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: When the refundable portion of the tax is paid back at the time called for, will it be paid back in such a way that it will constitute income under the ordinary regulations of the income tax act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have had an inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Taxable itself.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Taxable itself, being refunded at the end of the war.
That was cleared up.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was not in the chamber when it was. In any event, I have had an inquiry from one or two sources with respect to the matter. I understand that business houses and others are not allowed to set up this refundable portion of the tax as an asset for certain purposes. More than that, there is some fear that when it is refunded it will also be taxable a second time. Could the minister give us some light on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I made a statement in regard to the companies. It is not taxable again. They have saved it out of their earnings; it comes back free of tax.
I am not clear on the two per cent interest on it. I think that is taxable; but the question is, in what year it is taxable? The two per cent is taxable.
Is it not a return of principal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; the tax itself is a return of principal. But the two per cent interest on it is not.
The interest would be taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

May I
ask the minister about the change he is making now under this resolution, as to a spouse and her husband. Did I not see somewhere that after he turned that down last session in the legislation which was passed, it was put into effect? An announcement was made to the press that it was done or that it would be done by some regulation. What was the authority for that? Perhaps it has not been done yet, and this is to give effect to it. Will it be made retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was never an announcement that it would be done.
I saw in the papers that you were to do it. Maybe it was not authorized.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no announcement by the government or by anyone on behalf of the government that that would be done, until I announced it this year.
Will the minister give consideration to the letter I read with regard to the soldiers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, I will give it consideration, but I do not want to hold out too much

hope on that. A request of that kind is presented in this light, that if it is not done the soldier's insurance will lapse. There are two chances that it will not lapse. One is that the soldier will pay it himself; the other, that the parent will pay it for him. He has to pay a great many things which he cannot set off against these refundable taxes. But I will give the point some consideration.
This section, from what the minister said in his budget 'address is retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
I do not happen to see the one regarding annuities. That is included elsewhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
