speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The committee will
revert to resolution 14:
14. That the tax payable by a corporation shall be paid by twelve monthly instalments commencing in the sixth month prior to the close of its fiscal period
(a)	as to the first eleven months, one-twelfth of the estimated tax, having regard to the previous or anticipated current year's income, applying the current year's rates, and
(b)	as to the twelfth month, the balance of the tax payable, having regard to the income and applying the rates of the taxation year;
provided, however, that should any instalment paid in each month of the seventh to eleventh month, both inclusive, be less than one-twelfth of the tax actually found to have been due, such deficiency shall bear interest at the rate of 5 per cent per annum from the close of the company's fiscal period.
Shall resolution 14 carry?

Not
until the minister makes a statement as to what he is to do.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
This section will be
amended slightly, in that payments for the first six months may be estimated on the income for the previous year. If the tax is paid on the basis of one-twelfth of the tax calculated on the income for the previous year, that will be accepted without interest even though it is less than the tax actually payable on the income for the current year.

Income War Tax

Take the year 1943; if a company were of opinion at the beginning of 1943 that the year's income would not be as large as it was for 1942, would they pay on what they thought the 1943 income would be?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
It must be remembered
that companies are not on the pay-as-you-go method. In 1943 they will be paying on the 1942 income. A company whose year ends December 31, 1943, would start paying tax on the 1943 income in July, 1943. If they estimate their 1943 tax on the basis of the 1942 income and pay one-twelfth of that each month, no interest will be added, even though the payment may be under one-twelfth of the tax eventually found due.
Then we come to the period at the end of their fiscal year. At that time they know almost definitely what the year's income is, amd they will then be required to pay one-sixth per month of the balance that is owing on. the tax for 1943. They have already paid six months, and they have six months to pay in the following year. They will be required each month to pay one-sixth of the tax that remains due. There will be interest charged on any underpayment in that period, and that interest will be at the rate of five per cent from the end of the fiscal period. Even though the underpayment is made in January, February or March, the five per cent interest will be dated back to the end of the fiscal period.
Why do you do that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Otherwise the penalty
would be almost insignificant, if in the eleventh month they underpay there would be only one month's interest added to that payment.

It
might be that even in January or February they would not be quite sure of the income. It is not fair to date the underpayment back. It might amount to something considerable for some big companies.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
They would know fairly
accurately at the end of the year what their income for the year was, although their audited statements would not be prepared.

I
still think it is unfair, because if a parent company depended upon subsidiary companies to get in their returns they might not know until after February in many cases. At the
present time, on account of the shortage of accountants, it is very hard for companies to get their books audited.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I quite agree they-would not have their statements audited. But they have had the use of the money that is short-paid, and they would be paying five per cent interest on it from the time they should have known what their tax liability is, namely, from the end of the fiscal period.

Is there any consultation with the taxpaying public with respect to this or similar provisions? In the United States there is a practice of holding hearings on taxation bills such as this. I often wonder whether business is ever consulted through the chamber of commerce or similar bodies before these provisions are brought down in parliament. Or is it only afterwards that there is consultation? I know representations are often made to the Minister of Finance prior to his bringing down the budget, but those are made only in anticipation. They are not really consulted at all, are they?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Oh, yes; there are a good many consultations held both before and after the bringing in of the budget. Representations are very often made prior to the budget being brought down.

Was it ever considered that during the year and while parliament is in session people might come here and ask the banking and commerce committee to hear evidence in connection with their problems? You cannot treat every company on the same basis. I am not so concerned about the five per cent interest charge, except for the matter' of fairness. But there are some companies that do not know what their income is until some time after the close of the year.
I might give an illustration. I know a little about the casualty insurance business. Take it just in connection with automobile insurance; there are so many factors entering into the writing of that insurance that it takes the companies some time to determine their profits. At the present time there are fewer automobiles on the roads; there is less exposure to risk, but on the other hand rates have been lowered so much that the insurance companies do not know whether they will make a profit or not. In the insurance business you cannot tell before the end of the year what your profits will be for the year. The first part of the year is the premium paying time; the last part is the claims paying part.
Business wants to be consulted, not just by the minister; it wants to be consulted by such
Income War Tax

an organization as our banking and commerce committee. A great many of these problems could be ironed' out before that committee. So many different groups are interested in taxation. There is labour; they could come along and put their ideas before us, and the same with industry. A great deal of good would result if we did something along that line.

The minister says there is consultation with business, but is that not largely by way of asking for redress of grievances which arise out of the operation of laws, or proposed laws which have already been framed and brought down for introduction in parliament, and for rulings? That is bound' to happen, and it is all to the good that it should happen. I hope attention is paid, and I am sure it is, to the representations made by business; and I am confident that if in a given case relief can be granted, that will be done. What I was thinking about is this. Take this very resolution with which we are now dealing, concerning the payment of instalments of income tax by corporations. Was anybody ever consulted about that? After all, the taxpayer has some rights in the country, and his convenience should be considered in a degree. Or is this just an arbitrary * provision set up by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: While a great many representations are made as a result of legislation that has been passed, many representations are also made in regard to proposed legislation, in connection with matters that people think should be included in the taxing acts to assist industry or whatever taxpayers are being represented. Those representations are given very careful consideration before the budget is prepared.

Just apropos of what the minister has said, in making his budget speech the Minister of Finance said in effect that this was not the government's budget, that the government were prepared to listen to representations, and all that sort of thing. I protest against that; I say it is the government's budget; and unless the members of the House of Commons have more to say about the budget, more to say about the ways and means of raising money and so on before the budget is brought down^ it will continue to be the government's budget.

Would it not mean the adoption of a rather wide principle to ask representatives of corporations and other interests to come here and discuss details of taxation before the budget is brought down?
If that were done, then you ought to bring 
representatives of the wage and salary earners from whom deductions are to be made, and receive their representations.
That is what I suggested.	*
All interests should be consulted.
In that event, of course, you would do away with the time-honoured principle of the secrecy of the budget, or the foreshadowing of taxation before it is brought down.
That applies only to the tariff and matters like that.
It is not what I said.

It strikes me that if you are to invite representatives of chambers of commerce and of corporation interests, as was suggested just now, you must also invite all other interests to discuss the budget proposals before they are brought down. If we are to accept that principle it is all right, but I am suggesting that you could not invite representatives of chambers of commerce and of corporations, unless you invited all others interested in the budget proposals.

Last year I made the suggestion that we should give consideration to the principle of having similar public hearings on taxation measures to those they have in congress, and that the committee dealing with this question should hear every interest, including the treasury, as they do in the United States. Of course I realize that our constitutional set-up is quite different from that of the United States, and this invariably has been the stock answer to this proposal. But I should like to see the experiment at least tried in this country, so that we would not have so much of what I call trial-and-error taxation, as we have had it in the past. Take the question of the income tax proposals, which after all are the proposals of the treasury, because the Department of National Revenue is merely the collecting agent. If these proposals were submitted to the banking and commerce committee or some such body at public hearings, at which all parties and interests could appear and be heard, perhaps we would have a more democratic form of government than we have to-day. At the present time we have an autocratic form of government, or a bureaucratic form. The proposal has merit, though I see the difficulties which arise as a result of the difference in our constitutional

Income War Tax
set-uip. In the United States the; administrative or executive branch is not part of the legislative branch, as it is here. The answer always given is that the government, being responsible for taxation proposals, must formulate them and stand or fall by them. But in any case where secreicy is not required, as it is required in connection with tariff changes-in which case people might take advantage of the situation and abuse their privileges-I do not see why at least consideration should not be given to a proposal of this kind'. Certainly it would not do any harm, and alternative methods of taxation might be suggested.

As a matter of fact I did suggest that labour and other organizations should be .called in. It was not my idea that we should discuss the budget before it was brought down; but now we have the budget; it has been brought down, and I think it would be interesting to the people of the country if the banking and commerce committee could sit immediately and discuss these questions of taxation. Then we would be better prepared for next year; we might get rid of some of the bad things, and the government might be told how we could raise more money. I do not see any harm in taking such a step, and I think it might be given a trial.

The proposal advanced by the hon. member for St. Paul's differs from that made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, as I understood it; the two were essentially different. The objection I raised to the suggestion of the hon. member for York-Sunbury does not apply to that of the hon. member for St. Paul's. After all, however, the House of Commons is here, and it seems to me that we are more and more abrogating our powers and handing them over to outside organizations. I think the danger is that more and more the actual decisions may be removed from parliament. We should keep as much parliamentary control as we can, though the suggestion that taxation be criticized after it has been introduced has not the same objectionable features that the other proposal had.
The trouble is that you never get anywhere by postexamination.

When I offered my suggestion I had in mind the good that came out of the work of the banking and commerce committee in 1939, when it made a thorough examination into the question of money and finance. I think the minister recognizes the good work that was done by that committee
at that time, and that was exactly what I had in mind when I was speaking about the question of taxation. It was not a question of what the government should bring down, but a question of the various principles of taxation involved; for, after all, most of us do not understand the principles of taxation. We do not know; we have not the figures to show us. We do not know what the result might be if we put a big tax on cosmetics or some other unnecessary articles, as Great Britain has done. We do not know what would happen if a 100 per cent tax were placed on non-essential articles such as has been done in Great Britain. The results might be very satisfactory, and might bring in a great deal of money. I have the principle of taxation in mind, and it is my view that it might be a good idea to have the banking and commerce committee call witnesses to discuss this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I move, in amendment:
That resolution No. 16 of the resolutions to amend the Income War Tax Act be amended by deleting the word "current" after the words "as a deduction against" in the fifth line thereof.

What is the effect of
that amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The word "current" comes
out; that is all. The purpose of the amendment to resolution 16 is to allow companies to carry forward their expenditures on off-property explorations and drilling in>
the event of a company's income in the year in which an expenditure was incurred not being sufficient to absorb fully the expenditures made. This is given effect to by deleting the word "current" in the phrase which says that these expenditures may be allowed as a deduction against current income. Provision will then be made in the law to enable a company to take it as current expense or take it as a deduction against a succeeding year's income, where the current year's income is not sufficient to absorb the full expenditure.
This is one of the oil sections which, I fear, are rather controversial, and the consideration of which will occupy a considerable time in the committee. I might point out, however, that they are designed to give encouragement to the search for oil, and the development of oil resources in Canada, so greatly needed at the present time.

Before
the discussion becomes general, and for the benefit of those of us who are not familiar with oil-drilling, will the minister be good enough to make a general statement with respect to the government's proposals. Then, if he is in a position to do so, will he summarize in general what the objections are? I have been deluged1 with a mass of material against these proposals, and I must confess that, not being familiar with the business, I do not understand them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have every sympathy with the hon. member, and an acute appreciation of his difficulties. This is one of the most perplexing and complex questions with which we have had to deal. I, like him, have been deluged with representations from all quarters and all interests.
The object of these oil resolutions is to give some encouragement by lessening the taxes of companies searching for oil and carrying out exploration.

What
amelioration is given by these resolutions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Very considerable, indeed.
But it is not enough to satisfy many people who are making representations. We have given a great deal of thought as to how far we should go. I shall not anticipate the issue which no doubt will speedily become apparent as speeches are made; but the general situation is that we are permitting a speedier write-off than would ordinarily take place, from the incomes of certain taxpayers, and the write-off of certain expenditures they otherwise would not be able to have at all. We are also changing depletion allowances for incorporated bodies and, in certain instances, we are changing depletion allowances for individuals.
I believe it will be said, with respect to this proposal, that it is favourable to the large companies, as opposed to the royalty companies. It will be urged that by these provisions the small man is being discriminated against.
I gathered that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I might as well bring out the point, because that is exactly what the issue is. It will have to be argued out. We do not think it is discriminatory, and we have tried our best to prevent any discrimination.
Surely the minister is not standing up for the big fellow, is he?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
He accused us of that the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not admitting that for one minute. There will be amendments. The provisions are designed to get one result-oil.

The minister has cited in a general way a number of resolutions, but would he tell us the concrete position that at present obtains under the law with respect to these operations and then tell us what is proposed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would take threequarters of an hour.
It might be worth while.

I wish to commend the Minister of Finance for the sympathy he has shown for the oil industry. The budget of a year ago proved disastrous to the industry; the present budget will remove many of the injustices. However, in my opinion there are still some injustices which should be removed. I think it would simplify matters if the minister would consent to resolutions 16 and 17 being discussed together because they both deal with oil.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think we can avoid that.

The concessions granted by these resolutions can be taken advantage of only by the large companies. Under resolution 16 a company that drills a dry hole may offset those drilling costs against its income assessment. It costs $200,000 to drill a well, so that only the company with an assessable income of $200,000 would be able to offset the full cost of drilling a well against its income tax assessment. The small company cannot do this. A company with an income of $5,000 could offset only $2,000 on the cost of drilling a dry hole, and $2,000 would not go far in drilling.
I do not suggest that the government is too generous to the large companies, because it is not. It is only being fair to these companies. If a company drills for oil and meets with a loss, it should have the right to offset the losses sustained in one well against the profits of another. Banks are allowed to do this. If a bank lends money to two debtors and one fails to pay his debt, I believe the bank may offset the loss on the one against the profit on the other. This applies to most other lines of business; it is the only fair and proper thing to do so far as the oil industry is concerned.
As I say, the small companies cannot take advantage of this provision; for that reason they are not being fairly dealt with. I suggest to the minister that he allow a number of small companies or individuals to form a syndicate. Supposing twenty companies or individuals clubbed together and raised $10,000 each, they would then have $200,000 with which to drill a well. If the well proved to be a dry hole they should be permitted to charge their losses against their individual assessments, the same as the large companies are doing. That would prove very helpful to the industry because a number of small investors are ready to invest in oil.
You have to depend upon the little fellow to do the lion's share of wildcatting, as it is called. The big companies do not drill discovery wells; they do not wildcat; they do not pioneer. When the prospector or the small company brings in a well, the large company comes in and either acquires that well or acquires property on the structure. The large company gets into production with little or no risk. It does not go out and take chances the way the little fellow does. It is the little fellow who does the spade work in all mining operations. I believe the same is true in the United States. I should like to quote from an address delivered by Mr. Harold L. Ickes before the annual meeting of the independent petroleum association of America held at Wichita, Kansas. The statement was reported in Canadian Oil and Gas of October, 1942, and is as follows:
Especially do I want you to know that I realize the importance of the independent producer, both in peace and in war. The very term "independent" seems somehow symbolic of the American birthright of free opportunity. In saying that I find no criticism of the so-called major companies which, with only an occasional exception, have given devoted and patriotic service to our war programme, and have shown the finest kind of cooperation, and even when at times it has not been to their financial advantage. And yet I suspect that I shall always feel a warm affection for the little fellow and have a sympathetic interest in his problems. We must always have the independents, the little fellows, in all lines of endeavour in this country of ours. Without them, something would go out of the bone and fibre of America.
If we have needed you before, if we shall need you to-morrow we need you particularly to-day. Upon you we must depend for the lion's share of the wildcatting. To you we must look for the squeezing of the last possible drop of oil from our older wells through secondary recovery, now more essential than ever before. . . . For my part, I pledge you that your interests will always be protected scrupulously.
The reason, for the little fellow taking all the chances is obvious. The big company is managed by a board of directors who are financiers. They realize that the relation-

ship between the directors on the one hand and the company on the other and between the directors and the shareholders is a fiduciary one. They realize that it is their duty to be most conservative and guarded in the investment of the company's capital. They cannot afford to take chances with the company's money the same as they would with their own. If they wish to take a flier with their own money, well and good. But they have to handle the company's money conservatively and put it in safe and sound investments. For that reason it is not the big fellow that does the speculating, .prospecting or wildcatting. It is the, little fellow who does it, and unless something is done for the little fellow he will be driven out of the industry. I have already suggested one course that might be followed, namely, to allow the little fellows to form a syndicate and offset the total of their development costs, should they strike a duster, against their personal assessments. In that way they would be encouraged to speculate, take a chance and develop the oil industry.
The prospector who goes out and spends his money in this way is entitled to a generous return on the money invested. A committee of the United States senate used these words in a report a few years ago:
The prospector for mines, or oil and gas, frequently expends many years and much money in fruitless search. When he does locate a productive property and comes to settle, it seems unwise and unfair that his profit he taxed at the maximum rate as if it were ordinary income attributable to the normal activities of a single year.
I implore the minister to give the wildcat operator and the courageous explorer a chance. They hazard all their capital every day and all day long, and neither their taxes nor their burdens should be made too onerous.
I wish to say a word with regard to royalty companies. Since the royalty company may not be known to some members of the house- it probably is to a few-perhaps I should say a word as to the nature of the royalty company. All hon. members understand the workings of the ordinary company to which we refer as the share company. When a company is about to drill for oil it secures a location, and then the share company sets out to sell shares in order to raise the capital to do the drilling. But the royalty company does not do that. The royalty company goes out and sells shares, not in the capital of the company, but in the production to be obtained from an oil well. The reason for their proceeding in that way is this. When oil was first drilled for in Turner valley a company would drill, strike a well and get big production. Then, thinking

they were pretty wise, the company would drill a second well which might prove to be a dry hole. Then they would drill a third well, and so on, until all the money they made in the first profitable well was used up, and the poor shareholder got no return for his money. Therefore they devised this scheme of raising money from the sale of royalties. They sell royalties in a single well; a man knows when he buys a royalty in that well that the profits from the well cannot be used in any other way than to. be paid back to him and the other royalty holders. The practical working out of it is on this basis. After a site is selected, a three-party agreement is drawn up. The drilling company is the party of the first part. It undertakes to drill the well, recover the oil from it, sell the oil, and turn the realizations from that well over to a trust company. The trust company is the party of the second part. In turn, the trust company distributes the net realizations from that well among the royalty holders who are the parties of the third part. In that way the royalty holders know they are getting their money back and that it will not be reinvested by a board of directors.
A great deal of the development in the Turner valley oil field in the last few years has been carried on by royalty companies. At the present time the royalty companies are being put out of business. They cannot carry on under this scheme because, if they drill a well and get a dry hole, they have no assessable income against which they can assess the cost of drilling that dry hole; they have not a dollar of assessable income. For that reason they cannot take advantage of this concession. I had an accountant figure out for me how this taxation works out on the average well in Turner valley. He has taken a well which produces 300,000 barrels. The average for the first year would be 325 barrels a day. It is financed by the sale of eighty net royalties of $3,000 each, and that well, after all taxes are paid, shows a loss of $40,000. I should say, though, that it is figured out on last year's depletion allowance of twenty per cent, which is increased this year to thirty-three and one-third per cent. But the company I speak of, under that investment, would mahe no return on its money; it would not get all its investment back; it would lose $40,000. I have the figures prepared by the accountant to show how this is worked out. It may be that hon. members would be interested, and with the permission of the committee I would place them on Hansard.

These figures deal with an average well in Turner valley. If the average well is to make a loss in that way; if it is to be taxed to such an extent that it cannot make a profit but on the other hand suffers a loss, I suggest that something is wrong. I think it would be well if the minister would have his departmental mining engineer, or some person qualified to look into the matter, see what would be fair and reasonable under the circumstances, and then exempt from* 1 taxation small wells, say wells in Turner valley starting in with an initial production of 400 barrels.
Four hundred barrels in what length of time?

Four hundred
barrels a day at the initial production. It may be that that would be a reasonable amount to be allowed in the Turner valley field. Of course, in some other fields where one does not have to drill so deep-in our district we have to drill to a depth of seven, eight or nine thousand feet in order to get production-the costs would be less and the amount could be lowered. The amount fixed should have some relation to the depth it is necessary to drill in order to get oil in a particular field.

I make this suggestion as one which would be helpful to the industry and not unfair to the government. Certainly it is most unfair to tax capital investments, which is what is being done under the present system. It is not so bad under the current budget as it was under the last, but it is bad enough yet.
I submit that, by driving the small investor and the royalty companies out of the field in this way the government will lessen the income to be derived from this source. Without the small investor it will not be possible to get the development which would otherwise be had; if you do not get the development you cannot get the production, and if you cannot get the production you will not receive the income taxes, so that revenue will suffer. The men in the field will suffer too.
On the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains extending from the United States boundary to Alaska the outlook for oil is excellent. At many points in that area oil has oozed from the ground and can be seen floating on the water. The possibilities of enormous production are tremendous. I submit that the government should do something to help that industry. To encourage small investors woulfi assist a great deal, because we have numbers of idle rigs; we have the men, for there is a

good deal of unemployment in Calgary and the area generally; we have the crews; we have good drilling oil sites and the capital is available if it is given a chance.
I am very glad that the Minister of Munitions and Supply has come into the chamber, because I want him to get the benefit of what I am. saying. I see by the paper that a crown company has recently been organized. I hope that at a very early day the Minister of Munitions and Supply will let us know the plans of the company. It is important to the oil industry of Alberta that we know as soon as possible, so that plans may be made accordingly by the industry.

He *
should tell us to-night.

He probably will. Give him time. I say that in view of the immense possibilities for oil in the area of which I am speaking, the government should do something to stimulate production. The excessive taxes of last year have made it impossible for some companies to carry on. One company expected to reach oil at 7,500 feet. It raised $196,000 to drill; it got down to a depth of 8,949 feet; and it was closed down last December on account of shortage of money. All the indications point, I am informed, to the likelihood of good production being obtained from this well if the company can only drill to the point of production; but as I say, they were short of money and had to close down last December. People who had money to invest were afraid of the taxation which was imposed after the well was started. This made it impossible for them to finance further. It may be that this is a well which should be drilled deeper to production. I do not say it is; it may be. The government should send its mining engineers or geologists and investigate. If they conclude that it should be drilled to production, then the government should assist in the drilling of that well to production in order to help the industry at this time.
In what way could they help? I suggest two ways. One would be to lend money to the company, to be repaid out of the first production. The other would be for the government to buy shares in the company and take its chance with the other share or royalty holders in the company.
Another well is drilled to a depth of 8,000 feet and drilling is still going on. From the structure I understand that the prospects are good. But the company has no money to complete the well. They can tell approximately how much further they will have to go and can estimate in a measure what it will cost.
Mr. MaeNICOL: Are the wells in close proximity?

No; they are in different structures.
Mr. MaeNICOL:	But both in Turner
valley?

No; one is in Turner valley; the other is outside the valley. This company has drilled to a depth of 8,000 feet. It started drilling before this excessive taxation was imposed. Owing to the excessive taxation it cannot raise further money to complete the drilling and1 will have to close down soon unless it gets assistance in some way.
A third1 well is down 7,350 feet. This well has noit been stopped by reason of excessive taxation. In this case the manager of the company met with an unfortunate accident as a result of which he was unable to superintend further drilling operations and was also unable to complete the financing. But the prospects there are good. In fact they have reached production but not on a commercial scale. I had occasion to visit that well not long ago, and I have a picture here of what I saw. The well must be capped in order to prevent the oil and1 gas from escaping. When the well is uncapped the pressure of the gas is so great that it blows the oil fifty or sixty feet into the air. From the pictures I have distributed hon. members will see how it works. This is another well that should be investigated. If as a result of investigation it is concluded that the prospects are good, the well might be drilled to a greater depth in order to ascertain whether it is capable of commercial production.
In each of the three cases I have mentioned drilling the well and getting production would open up a new structure; the opening of that new structure would pave the way for oil development on quite a large scale on each of those three structures. Therefore I submit that it is very important that the structure should be proved.
There are others in the same position. When these companies started to drill we did not have the excessive taxation which was imposed last session. These men invested their money and started drilling operations assuming that they would be given a run for their money. Then, when the excessive taxation came into effect investors closed down; they will no longer invest, and that is the position we are in.

The concession granted under section 16 applies only to wells spudded- in since January 1, 1943. I urge the minister to delete that limitation and let the concession apply to those wells that have been commenced. That would do a great deal to stimulate production, because wells commenced before January 1, 1943, should have a chance. I have been told that in the case of some of the wells commenced before January 1, 1943, the companies would be better off from a financial point of view by abandoning the present hole and drilling alongside of it, in order to get the benefit of this resolution. I urge the minister to give that matter careful consideration.
The royalties taken by the government of Alberta amount to Wfe per cent. That is a gross royalty taken on total production. Being a gross royalty, it is an enormous tax. If the minister would treat the companies more fairly and grant them reasonable taxation and reasonable concessions, then the drillers might go to the Alberta government and say, Mr. Aberhart, see what the dominion government is doing; they are treating us generously now we want you to postpone your royalties until we get enough production, to repay preproduction costs. They could then make that request with a good deal of reason. If the dominion government were acting generously and fairly with the companies, they could then ask the provincial governments to act fairly and generously as well.
I wish now to say a word or two with regard to the price of oil. In the past the oil companies received SI.50 a barrel for their oil at the well head. A few days ago this was raised to $1.65 a barrel. That was helpful, and the industry feels grateful for it. But I wish to point out that the dominion government is importing a great deal of oil and- paying subsidies on that importation. I know the minister is anxious to preserve the price ceiling, and I hope he will be able to maintain it. It is important that it should be maintained, and I shall not urge that the price ceiling be removed. But the government at the present time is paying a good deal of money by way of subsidies and bonuses in order to bring in oil from the United States. I suggest that instead of paying bonuses to United States companies the minister pay part of the bonuses to the operators in Turner valley, and give them a chance to do the producing. If they are given this chance, there will be less oil imported and we shall get more oil from Turner valley and the eastern slopes of the Rockies, where there is so much of it. I should
'Mr. G. H. Rosa.1
like to read here what George C. Cross had to say on this matter in Western Business of April 2, 1943. He refers to the attitude of the government as "one of Canada's war-time mysteries," and goes on to say:
At this stage in the war the paramount consideration should -be how to get oil the quickest way, provided the _ source may be relied upon continuously. The inconsistency in the situation rests in the fact that Canada is importing oil from United States fields at much higher prices and paying transportation costs, while drilling equipment in Turner valley remains idle.
It would hardly be possible for the refined products from the imported oil to be sold within the Canadian price ceiling unless the Canadian government absorbs the increase in price. In fact Hon. J. L. Ilsley, Minister of Finance, told the House of Commons Thursday that import subsidies on petroleum were responsible for a substantial part of the $80,000,000 included in the estimates for import subsidies for the current year. Why not devote this money instead to developing Canada's own oil resources, thereby relieving the hard-pressed United States oil industry of one of the drains upon it and also releasing tank cars for more vital work? The subsidy principle has had to be applied to strategic minerals and lumber. Oil is just as essential.
Allowing nearly half the drilling rigs in Turner valley to remain idle when there are plenty of proven sites for them to drill has been one of the inexplicable phases of Canada's generally excellent war programme. The sad but necessary commentary upon the action taken this, year is that it was so long delayed that the stimulation it should give to drilling of wells in proven areas will be too late to help out the oil supply situation in Canada in this critical year of 1943. To reach the oil reservoir in the Madison limestone of Turner valley takes nine months or longer, depending on the difficulties encountered. But if idle rigs are put to work within the next few weeks the increased production should be a factor in whittling down the amount of the import subsidy Mr. Ilsley will have to provide for 1944.
