I have something further to say, Mr. Chairman, but I will bring it in later on in the debate.

I do not come from an oil country as does the hon. member who immediately preceded me, but I do come from a part of western Canada which is very much interested in the development of industry and which certainly is hopeful that a field will be developed somewhat closer to the city of Saskatoon than Turner valley. I may add that many people in my city and in the surrounding country have in past years invested their savings not only in Turner valley but in some closer fields which they hope to see developed.
Unquestionably petroleum products are urgently required, as I think the minister has made quite clear. He made that statement in his budget speech and repeated it this evening when, as I understood him, he said that the purpose of these changes was to bring about more oil. What he wants, and what this country wants, is the development of our resources so that we may have substantial quantities of this great natural product which is so necessary, particularly in war time. May I quote what the minister said during his budget address, because I wish to make some reference to the language he used at that time. At page 859 of Hansard the minister is reported to have said:
Included in the income tax proposals are a number intended to encourage the search for new sources of oil in Canada during the next two years. The government recognizes the urgent necessity under present emergency conditions of expanding our oil production and, if possible, of discovering new oil producing areas in various parts of Canada. Success in the search for oil depends upon a combination of experience, skill and good judgment, as well as capital and good luck; it is essential therefore to bring into the search all we can of those with the necessary skill and experience. We desire to remove so far as possible any barriers which taxation may impose in the way of this search for oil.
Not only do we require oil for the purposes of war, but we require it also for peace-time purposes. We should take advantage of the
situation which has arisen through the war to do everything we can to encourage production of oil in Canada. Most of what I shall say this evening I must confess has been represented to me, because I have no technical knowledge of the problem. I am informed, however-and I believe the figures are correct -that we produce only about 15 per cent of the petroleum products we require. One of the drawbacks in the development of petroleum fields during the years immediately preceding the war was that crude oil could be brought so cheaply from the United States that there was not sufficient incentive to develop our own fields to the extent possible, or to the extent that some of us in Canada would have liked to see done.
That condition has now changed. It is much more difficult to obtain crude oil from the United States, and it becomes imperative to develop our own resources to the limit. I suggest that we should take advantage of every opportunity we now have of developing our industry to the point where, in peace time, we can produce oil at a cost comparable with that of the product brought in from the United States.
May I emphasize that the important factor, so far as our war effort is concerned, is that of getting the product. After'all, the financial arrangements made, the tax structure and all that sort of thing are not important if we do not get results. Even at the risk of upsetting some of our financial schemes we should work out some plan under which we would get physical results. We should not worry too much about the financial aspect of the problem, so far as the government's tax policy is concerned.
It seems to me that in the past the government's policy of taxation has discouraged the drilling of wells. I realize that the hon. member who preceded me said that these provisions are now inserted in an attempt to a certain extent to remedy what I might describe as discouragement, so far as drilling is concerned. But there are two things to remember. In the first place the provisions do not go far enough. They do not provide the necessary encouragement-and I mean real encouragement-for the development of what has been referred to as wildcatting. In the second place the provisions are much more helpful to the large companies and are of comparatively little assistance to the small operator, or the person who actually has pioneered in Canada's oil industry; because we must remember that it was the small person, the small investor, who put his money into these companies, who had the most to do with the development of oil
Income War Tax

in Canada. We may call it the gambling instinct, if we like. For years I have known people who have what I would describe as a yen for going into oil investments. They are continually getting their bits of money together and investing it in these cooperative ventures. Then they go out in an endeavour to locate a well and actively to develop it. I liken the situation somewhat to that of a person who gambles in mechanical devices. There were those who, when they could do so, and when such procedure was not against the provisions of the criminal code, were always putting their nickels into slot machines. Perhaps the results were not the same, but the instinct which prompted the action was the same. A person would persist in gambling his nickels in the machine in the hope that at some time he might hit the jack-pot. These small oil men are continually putting their money into these ventures in the hope that some day they, too, may hit the jack-pot.
The taxing policy of the administration has been such that, even if they did win, they lost; consequently they had no more incentive to gather up their money and invest it in this way. We all know what a small chance the person had who gambled against the slot machine, and he has a similar chance, so far as oil wells are concerned. Then, if we are to say to him /'Even if you do win, we will take your winnings away from you," we will certainly discourage him from collecting the money he formerly collected for purposes of investment. These investors have been discouraged through the financial and tax policy, and the price-ceiling policy of the government. In saying that I am not making any special criticism of government policy at the present time. I shall deal with government policy, bit by bit, as I go along. Nevertheless the result has been that these people have been discouraged.
The primary necessity is to get production. The handicaps in development of wells and getting production appear to be entirely financial. I am informed that there are those who have the experience and the oil-drilling equipment, and they have the knowledge necessary to carry on their work. But their handicap is that they believe the returns are not commensurate with the risks they must take.
As I see it, there are two ways of producing oil in Canada. First of all, it could be done by public ownership. The government could go into the oil business. It could send out drilling equipment and buy up the fields. It could endeavour to do its own exploration, taking the risks and the results as they might develop. The other way, of course, is through private enterprise. If we have neither public

ownership nor private enterprise which has received sufficient encouragement to carry on the work, we cannot possibly get results. We must have one or the other.
So far as I am concerned, I do not believe public ownership should be the way to do it, and I make that statement for several reasons. I shall not discuss at length the questions connected with the development of resources through public ownership. I must point out, however, that I do not think it could be worked out from the point of view of administration, nor dio I believe the great bulk of Canadian taxpayers would want to gamble their money on the development of anything so hazardous.
But there are all kinds of private investors who are prepared to put their money into this type of venture. It seems to me that if they are willing to do it and to take the risks they should be given encouragement. And when I refer to private enterprise I am referring to enterprise on the part of the small man, the man who will invest his money in an independent fashion and who will endeavour to get his capital back through the development of royalty companies and so on.
I believe there has been a small attempt made to develop these resources through public ownership. The hon. member who preceded me referred to a crown company which has been set up. Although I do not know the details of it, I have been informed that the purpose is to do certain exploratory work. The setting up of such a company certainly would be open to criticism in peace time. I do not suggest that is necessarily so now, but I do say the job cannot be done through public ownership, or a crown company, unless we are willing to gamble money from the treasury of Canada in the development of all of our vast resources. I understand, too, that recently the Canadian National Railways have been investing funds in the exploration of certain fields in western Canada. Again that is all very well in its way, but to all intents and purposes this is a public company. It is owned by the government and the money of the taxpayers is behind it. I suggest that rather than doing the thing piecemeal by having one crown company here and another company wholly owned by the government there, it would be better to go the whole hog and encourage these small people to whom I have referred to do it for us.
The fact is that as a result of the tax policy of the administration for the last number of years we have been retrogressing instead of progressing so far as the development of oil is concerned. I am informed, and I

Income War Tax
have every reason to believe that my information is correct, that fewer wells are now being drilled in Turner valley than have been drilled since 1937. In 1937 the crude development was just getting under way. The reasons are obvious. As I have mentioned before, there has not been the encouragement that there should have been.
There are several things the administration proposes to do to encourage such development. One was referred to in the budget speech. It is not part of the resolutions; I believe it comes in by way of a change ini the schedule. It is proposed that pre-production expenses of any oil well may be written off against the income from it. The change provides that forty per cent may be written off in the first year, thirty per cent in the second, twenty per cent in the third, and the remaining ten per cent in the fourth. That will be a great help. Under the old schedule it began with thirty per cent. It was possible that a company might find that the ultimate decline would prove that an oil well would not pay at all, so that the tax paid on the first year's income would turn out to be a tax on capital instead of a tax on income.
There are other suggestions which were contained in the budget speech. I quote from page 859 of Hansard as follows:
In the case of wells commenced-"spudded in" I believe is the correct term-between January 1 of this year and March 31 of 1945, preproduction expenses may be written off as rapidly as the operator desires.
I am informed1 that this was the United States method used in peace time and it should1 have been available here long before. There is no reason why it should be limited to wells started only in the next two years. It ought to apply to all wells. It is quite obvious that people in this country will not take the long chances they have to take in this very precarious industry if this is to be limited to a period of two years.
The next change in regulation mentioned in the budget speech is the increase from fifteen per cent to twenty-five per cent in the depreciation rate to be applied to all depreciable assets used in oil production, including oil drilling equipment. As I understand it, the purpose of this change, is to endeavour to bring into line with actual experience the depreciation rate that is to be allowed. I am informed that this still falls far short of the actual experience so far as oil drilling equipment is concerned; that the actual rate of depreciation is in excess of twenty-five per cent.
The next provision to which I should like to refer is mentioned also in the budget
speech. This provides for an increase in the special war-time depletion allowance from twenty per cent to thirty-three and a third per cent in respect of royalty payments received by investors from wells spudded in during the period January 1, 1943, to March 31, 1945. I understand that this is done in order to alleviate some of the retroactive principles of the budget of last year. . I believe it was found that the investment of money in royalty companies had practically stopped.
It seems to me that if you restrict these concessions to such a short period you cannot expect small finance to develop these resources. Owing to the discouragement that they have suffered they have gone out of this industry. The encouragement provided by a provision like this is not sufficient to bring them back again.
The next provision is set forth in resolution 17, which reads:
17. That exploration expenses incurred during the period January 1, 1943, to March 31, 1945, by companies formed for the exploration and drilling for oil may be accumulated and allowed as an expense against the income from any well found hereafter by such company.
It has been represented to me, and I believe correctly, that this provision will help only the large companies, the ones that have plenty of money and can continue to develop their oil fields and prospect over a number of years. The situation might easily arise with a small company with limited capital that it might drill a number of wells and find that its capital had run out. It would not be able to take advantage of this resolution. But another company with unlimited capital could go on exploring and drilling, and after five, six, even eight or ten years might bring in a well against which all the expenses of the previous drilling could be charged. The resolution reads, "as an expense against the income from any well found hereafter by such company". I am not objecting to that provision; I am simply saying that it does not help the small man. Someone suggested! to me, I cannot remember whether it was inside or outside the house, that whereas resolution 16 would help the large company, resolution 17 should help the small one. So far as I can see it will not help them very much for the reasons I have given.
The next provision to which I wish to refer is resolution 16 which the chairman has read. I shall not read it all again but only the last few words, starting in the middle of line 5:
. . . whose principal business is the production and/or refining and/or marketing of petroleum and/or petroleum products.
Income War Tax

If there ever was a provision that gave the advantage to the big companies, certainly that one does because, generally speaking, it is the big companies whose principal business is the production and refining of petroleum and/or petroleum products. Why the opportunity to search for oil in Canada should be restricted to those who are already engaged in the business, . not of searching, but of producing, refining or marketing is difficult for me to understand. To my mind the references I have made are indicative of the fact that the conception behind these tax concessions is the conception of the big company and the big interest. The idea does not seem to have occurred to the minds of those who conceived such concessions that they should encourage the small people. I know the minister has received representations by the dozen through the mail, but I suggest to him that he ought seriously to reconsider the position so far as the small people are concerned. I think he should give a full statement to the committee as to the reason why the whole trend seems to be only along the line of giving concessions to the big companies.
One point has arisen which may be a partial explanation why the department feels that it should not go any further in this respect, namely, that if they go further with respect to the oil industry, other industries, those which are engaged in mining for minerals, for example, will feel that greater concessions should be made to them for the purpose of developing minerals. I recognize, of course, that minerals are very necessary to our war effort, but I also realize that there is an abundance of minerals in this country, and so far as the actual production is concerned there is not nearly the same degree of risk in the production of minerals as there is in the production of oil. It can be determined before a great deal of mining work has been done whether or not there are minerals under the ground, and certainly we have well established mineral deposits which are available in this country, some with difficulty perhaps; but, generally speaking, they are available, and it is more or less certain that they can be produced if the companies and the individuals concerned are prepared to go ahead. The development of oil, however, is one of the greatest gambles there is. You have to spend a great deal of money before you even know whether there is a possibility of oil, and time after time wells have been sunk only to find that there is no product there at all. The cost of exploration and of sinking these wells is tremendous in proportion to the chance of gaining any return. The fact that fewer wells 
have been developed and are being developed in the Turner valley in recent years seems to me conclusive proof that the policy which has been followed up to the present time by the department has been a faulty one. These amendments will correct it to a certain extent, but whether they go far enough to encourage oil development to the extent the administration wants to have it encouraged I do not know. I am afraid not, for some of the reasons I have given. It does seem to me that the administration might well consider taking further steps, not just doing as they did the other day, further increasing the price, because I do not believe the whole answer to the problem is to increase the price of oil. That would mean just another breach of the price ceiling, and as the hon. member who preceded me has pointed out, a great deal of money has been spent on subsidies to prevent breaches in the price ceiling.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: There was no breach in the price ceiling through the last increase in crude, for there was no increase in the price of the refined products. It was a squeeze between the producer and the refiner.

How the thing comes out in the long run I do not know, but I do know of many squeezes that have been executed between the producer and the manufacturer. How this one worked out so far as the price ceiling is concerned I do not know. Perhaps the minister might enlighten us a little further on that point. I presume there must be some kind of adjustment so far as these other companies are concerned.
I was about to suggest that we should adopt to a certain extent some of the methods which have been accepted in the United States. It has been suggested to me that we can easily get around any possibility of a breach in the price ceiling and' the possibility of the disruption of some of the other financial factors if we allow a greater depreciation allowance, with wildcatting costs being offset against the income of the searching companies. The position as I see it is this. A breach in the price ceiling not only will be open to a great deal of criticism but would have a disturbing effect on agriculture. I do not think we ought to do anything to disturb the agricultural position more than we can help, because, after all, the agriculturist is one of the most important producers in the country and he has enough troubles as it is without our doing anything which might possibly affect his costs of production. If a subsidy were paid it would not be of much help in encouraging the small people unless some arrangements were made for making it to a large extent tax-free.

Income War Tax
That is why I raise this suggestion which I know has been presented to the minister before, and I hope he will give it very careful consideration. My suggestion is that some arrangements should be made for a greater depletion allowance for these production companies on new production. If the minister would adopt the suggestion of some kind of depletion allowance on each barrel of oil which was produced, the encouragement would remain, and there would not be the possibility of an investor feeling that when he took a chance and spent another dollar, no matter what happened, it would be taken away from him by way of taxes.
I would ask that the minister seriously consider some of the suggestions I have made, particularly the matter of a depletion allowance.
I have thought the matter over very carefully, and1 I do not see how any of the alternative propositions could be properly worked out. If he would do it in the way I have suggested, he would avoid the possibility of a breach in the price ceiling; he would avoid offering an incentive which in fact is not an incentive at all, and at the same time nothing would be taken from the federal treasury, because these companies would be encouraged to produce more, whether in western Canada or in any other place where oil may be obtained. This would not only greatly benefit and assist us in our war effort but establish a permanent industry which would produce income over the years, and indeed, from a long-haul point of view, contribute far more revenue to the dominion treasury than the other policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question before he sits down?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is advocating an increased depletion allowance for operators-I suppose, a substantially increased one. Would that not give a large and unneeded benefit to present operators, whether large or small companies, and diminish to a marked degree the tax revenues of the country, without accomplishing anything so far as the present operators are concerned?

It quite possibly might, so
far as the big companies are concerned; I do not know about that. But it seems to me so very important that we increase production. As I mentioned before, at the present time the administration is so much worried about production that it has not only brought in these concessions but incorporated a crown company for the purpose of doing exploitation. The Canadian National Railways is spending the taxpayers' money in an endeavour to exploit this field. I am trying to work out some kind
of solution which will encourage the people who are ready to gamble their money-if you like to use the word "gamble"-to exploit these fields so that we shall not have to come into this matter from* a public ownership point of view.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But does not the hon.
gentleman think that he ought to work out something which would lead to a greater production of oil without giving benefits, at the expense of the public exchequer, to existing companies large and small, which the proposed increased allowance would do?

I quite agree with that, if
it can be done. But at the present time the main objective is production, and all of these concessions which have been made, with the exception of the one which was referred to in the budget speech and is related to the new schedule of twenty, thirty and forty per cent, are in favour of the big companies. So far as I can see, there is no concession which will help the small operator.

I trust the fact that I
come from that part of Canada which is the centre of the oil industry of the dominion will not cause it to be charged to my account that I am- parochial in my outlook or viewpoint so far as this problem is concerned. I reiterate what I said last year, when speaking to another bill affecting the oil industry, that I have no personal stake in it nor am I in any different position from that of any other Canadian citizen. I trust I shall be fair and dispassionate in my attitude toward this subject, as I believe our Minister of Finance is. We all are trying to seek a solution of what is a major problem confronting not only Canada but the allied nations in the conduct of this war. One needs only to think for a moment of what would happen to this country if our oil supply were cut off. Apart altogether from the inconvenience which we civilians now suffer in the ordinary activities of our lives, what would happen in so far as the fighting ability of our army, navy and air force is concerned if our oil supplies were cut off? The importance of oil is apparent to anyone who recalls the primary objective of the Germans in their invasion of Russia. The first object of attack was the Caucasus oil fields. Or turn to the other side of the globe: to what point did the Japanese drive? The oil sources in the East Indies. And to bring the matter closer home, need I remind hon. members how agitated and concerned we were on account of certain activities of our enemies along our east coast? These observations, relating to facts within the knowledge
Income War Tax

of all of us, show the importance of oil not only in time of peace but particularly in time of war. Where would the allied nations be to-day but for the oil resources and their availability to us south of the 49th parallel?
And in South America.

And in South America,
but more particularly immediately to the south of us.
I am forced to ask myself this question, which I am sure has occurred to every thoughtful Canadian: why is it that there is, or perhaps I should say there was, an abundance of supply available in the United States, although it is rapidly diminishing, while we in Canada have no such available supply, although geologists will tell you that the same oil fields continue along the east slope of the Rocky mountains all. the way from Mexico, up through the western states, into southern Alberta, and as far as the oil sandls of the Mackenzie river? The explanation is to be found in the attitude of the United States government to the. oil industry as such. The oil industry in the United States was a full grown giant before it was hit with taxation at all. Every encouragement was given to men to go out and gamble their money-and I use that term deliberately and advisedly-in exploring the oil resources of that country. It was as a result of that policy of unrestricted1 encouragement that there occurred the tremendous development of the oil industry in the United States, without which I doubt very much if the outlook in our present struggle would be as bright as it is to-day.
I look at the taxing legislation, because oil is essentially a money proposition. It takes big money; it takes wild -money to discover oil. WThy ? There is no means yet discovered to tell a man on the surface whether or not there is oil below, how far below, or in what quantity. Unlike any other industry, not excluding metalliferous mining, if you are to produce oil you must be prepared to gamble your whole capital investment of plant that is to produce the oil. On the eastern slope of the Rockies in Alberta, which is at present at least the major oil field-I was about to say of the British empire-the gamble is more hazardous and more extreme than in practically any other field, certainly on the north American continent, fraught with more hazard than attends oil exploration or development on any other part of the north American continent, and I think the same comparison applies to South America.
When the great republic to the south decided to tax the oil or petroleum industry, 
how did they go about it? I took the trouble to obtain Regulations 103 of the United States treasury department on income tax. I find under section 114-(3)- this:
In the ease of oil and gas wells the allowance for depletion under section 23 (m) shall be 27J per centum of the gross income from the property during the taxable year, excluding from such gross income an amount equal to any rents or royalties paid or incurred by the taxpayer in respect of the property. Such allowance shall not exceed 50 per centxxm of the net income of the taxpayer (computed without allowance for depletion) from the property, except that in no case shall the depletion allowance under section 23 (m) be less than it xvould be if computed without reference to ' this paragraph.
That is the taxing section for oil companies in the United States in peace-time. It has been in effect for a great number of years, and the United States congress has never altered that, despite the apparent abundance of oil in that country.
I wish to make a comparison later of that taxing section with ours. I suggest that the. situation in, which this country finds itself with respect to oil and petroleum is because we have not granted equal concessions, and even now the minister's proposals in regard to depletion allowance are not anything like comparable with the allowance made to similar companies in- the United States. Is it to be wondered at that even at this date we import eighty-five per cent of our oil; that we produce only fifteen per cent? I suggest that the state of the law as it has been heretofore and as is now proposed is responsible for the situation in which the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who- is most greatly concerned about this matter, finds himself at the present time.
Here is an interesting sidelight on the oil industi-y in Canada. When I started to look into this problem a few weeks ago I found that from 1905 to 1923 Canada paid a bounty, if you please, not a bonus but a bounty, to anyone who xvould produce a gallon of oil out of mother earth. The bounty was one and a half cents a gallon, which is equivalent to 52 1/2 cents a barrel. In 1923 the then minister of finance in his budget resolutions proposed to discontinue that bounty at the expiration of one year and that for the next ensuing year the bounty be cut in half, or to three-quarters of a cent a gallon, and at the end of 1926 be discontinued altogether. Why? Because the minister was fearful lest, on account of the discoxreries of oil in the west- we had Royalite No. 4 and some of these gas wells blowing-that we were on the eve of a tremendous oil development, and that so many gallons of oil would be produced that the federal treasury would be undermined.

Income War Tax
There is an interesting comment. If you read those debates you find that the one man who opposed the minister's proposals and said it would wreck the small oil industry which then existed in Canada near Sarnia and in the shale fields of New Brunswick was a man by the name of LeSueur who is now, I understand, president of the greatest oil company in Canada, Imperial Oil. Mr. LeSueur in the house asked that at least this bounty should be continued with respect to the first five barrels of oil that should be daily produced in any well. But the minister was adamant and refused to budge from his position, the bounty was discontinued in 1926, and from that time on the oil industry in Canada has been treated no differently from any other industry. I submit that that accounts very largely for the position in which we find ourselves to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Might I ask my hon. friend if the real development of oil in this country has not occurred since the bounty was dropped?
Yes, I grant that. But the minister does not mean to suggest that it was the dropping of the bounty that gave the impetus to the development of oil?

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: What did?

What did? The natural inclination of men to seek the pot of gold; the natural gambling instinct of certain men, of whom I do not claim to be one; the search for that elusive thing called petroleum which promises such rich rewards if you are lucky, and such tremendous losses if you are not.
When the budget resolutions were before the house last year an amendment to the income tax act was introduced in regard to the so-called royalty company, which is not a company at all but which the minister created in order to impose his tax, against which I protested at the time. I then prophesied that it would be a great deterrent to oil prospecting and developing in Alberta. The truth of that statement is best shown by the facts with regard to the condition of the Turner valley field at the present time. I take 1937 as my basis, because that was the beginning of the discovery of crude oil as such in Turner valley; the oil obtained from that field prior to that time was for the most part wet gas or pure gasoline. There are fewer wTells drilling in Turner valley to-day than there have been since 1937, when the crude development was just getting under way. Of the nineteen wells now drilling in Turner valley, eleven are being drilled by companies commonly referred to as independents, as differentiated from the integrated or major companies such as Imperial
Oil; seven are being drilled by major companies, and one is being drilled jointly. Within three months, unless the minister's proposals become as effective as he believes and hopes they will be and as I sincerely hope and would like to believe they will be, all but two of these wells will be finished. Only two new wells are in sight, and there is every prospect that Turner valley drilling will be virtually at a standstill within the next two or three months, since more than half of the wells now drilling will be finished within the next thirty days.
Do the wells now drilling give promise of producing oil?

Yes, Certainly. Be it said, too, that there are many wells in Turner valley closed down and not drilling, and I do not know of any drilling rigs that have been put to work recently. At no time since 1937 have there been more idle drilling rigs in Turner valley than there were at the end of March, before the minister's proposals were announced, and afterwards; and I do not know of any that have been put to work as a result of his proposals. Yet I for one devoutly hoped that the proposals would have had results.
Did I understand the hon. member to say that wells are now capped that were producers?

No; far from it. I
mean wells partly drilled and closed down, uncompleted.
Let me now go back to our legislation affecting oil wells. Heretofore oil fields have not been discovered, as one might suppose, by the large companies. I am informed and believe that four out of five of the major oil fields in the United States were discovered by the non-integrated companies as opposed to the major companies. The same story is true so far as Canada and Turner valley are concerned. If we had relied upon the large oil companies, Turner valley would probably never have been brought in. It was an old pioneer who gambled his all to bring in the first well in Turner valley; and after the Turner valley gas field as such was discovered, it remained for the independent companies to discover the crude oil potentialities of that field. In other words, had it been left to the integrated, major companies, Turner valley still would be half a mile wide by about a mile and a half long. It was the independent oil companies that extended the field by their wildoatting both south and north.
Income War Tax

I am concerned because the minister's proposals do not provide the incentives or the considerations or the concessions which they should to those people who in the past have been, are now, and I believe in future will be those to bring in new oil fields. Of the 204 wells in Turner valley at the present time, fifty-three are royalty-financed and eighty-one are independent company-financed. In other words, of the 204 wells in Turner valley, 134 have been drilled and are producing as a result of the investment, the enterprise and the gambling, if you will, of private individuals and small independent companies. Yet those 134 wells last year produced 65-8 per cent of the total crude oil production of Turner valley. As of the end of December 31, 1942, those wells had produced 70-7 per cent of the accumulated crude oil production from Turner valley, totalling 29,690,421 barrels.
Let us look at the other side of the question. Eight wells were jointly financed by independent organizations and the Imperial Oil Company. Sixty-two wells were drilled by the Imperial Oil group. In 1942 the joint Imperial-independent wells produced 343,303 barrels, or 3-6 per cent of the 1942 production. The sixty-two Imperial Oil company wells produced 2,963.475 barrels, or 30-6 per cent of the total 1942 production.
In other words, the royalty and independently-financed wells produced last year sixty-five per cent of production of Turner valley, and 70-7 per cent of the total aggregate production of crude oil from that field.
One would have thought that in the drafting of these resolutions more concessions would have been given to those companies, organizations and institutions which had given Canada such oil reserves as she now has, or had contributed thereto more largely than any other organizations, including the so-called major oil companies.
There is another interesting commentary I should like to make. Both ministers are interested in discovering oil-bearing strata. Production is not the problem. It is simple and easy to produce, once we know where the oil is located. Literally, oil is where you find it; and the question confronting both ministers is this: where do they want their money? Do they want it invested in government bonds, or in the search for oil? Which is their major problem to-day? Do they want money invested in Canada's war effort, or do they wish to have it spent in an endeavour to discover and produce what I submit we need much more than money?

Oil is war's greatest
munition.

Yes; it is the very lifeblood of our war effort. I submit there are two ways of getting oil. We can continue to buy it, as we are now doing, up to eighty-five per cent of our requirements; or we can drill for it and produce it, as we now dio to the extent of fifteen per cent of our requirements. Our present concern clearly indicates that oil is becoming more and more difficult to buy. Therefore we have to drill and produce. At this point our problem resolves itself into one of two ways of financing drilling operations-(1) the government doing the job, putting up the money and taking the chances, or (2) private business organizations doing the job, putting up the money and taking the chances. Which way does our government propose to do it? If the government intends to do the job, then those Canadians who have been instrumental in finding and developing the areas we have today, and in producing seventy per cent of the oil in the Turner valley field and ninety per cent of the oil in areas outside Turner valley, are through. The solution is found, and we can stop there. And I am afraid that is the position in which we find ourselves to-day. Independent companies are not drilling. Royalty companies are not drilling. I do not know of one oil well which has been financed since the minister's proposals introduced a year ago, and the only reason for this condition is the taxation measures of the government.
If private organizations and Canadians generally are to do the job, then we must recognize the risks and hazards involved. We must see that capital is remunerated for taking those risks, and give every consideration to methods and amounts of taxation imposed. Every barrel of oil produced in Canada is one barrel less on which we have to pay a subsidy.
The government is to be commended in that last fall it removed, in large measure, the customs tariffs against oil-drilling machinery and equipment. Those tariffs should have been removed years ago. It is estimated that every oil well in Turner valley has paid SIS,000 in taxes and customs duties on imported well-drilling equipment. All of these duties on necessary equipment have not yet been removed, as the hon. member for Calgary East pointed out earlier this evening.
The present minister is to be commended, too, for the other measures which he intimated would be covered by regulations, and are not included1 in these resolutions. I refer to the increased depreciation allowances. This is nothing new. Oil companies in the

Income War Tax
United States have enjoyed this concession in regard to depreciation for years. What applies in connection with ordinary industrial equipment and machinery has no application to oil well machinery and equipment on account of the nature and condition of the gas and sulphur content and its effect upon the equipment. It would seem that our tax structure is based) on the theory of what applies in other industries without regard to the facts which appertain to the particular industry under review.
With all due deference and subject to correction by the minister, I submit that the concession proposed in this resolution is not new. The concession provided by resolution 16 was available two years ago to companies which were producing and would undertake to drill wells on structures which were first approved by the government geologists. The procedure has been simplified. I ask the minister why this concession is limited to wells spudded-in during the period January 1, 1943, to March 31, 1945. Peradventure I have spudded-in my well on December 31, 1942, and I get none of the benefits of this resolution. There are not a few oil wells in Alberta which are considering the advisability of moving their rigging over to a different site to start anew in order that they may obtain the benefits of this resolution.
I read further that this concession applies only to companies whose principal business is the production and/or refining and/or marketing of petroleum and/or petroleum products. If we assume that such a company brings in a duster, it can write off forty per cent of the money it loses against its profits on other operations. Why should that concession be limited to any particular class of people or to any particular industry? Why not grant it to any company which will spend money in drilling for oil or to assist in drilling a well? Why not grant it to any individual who will invest $100,000 or $150,000? Who can go into the oil marketing business to-day with the restrictions that exist? Who could start up an oil refinery to-day in order to get the benefits of this resolution? It does not need too much imagination to see who will be able to take advantage of the benefits of resolution 16.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is one thing I think
I should add to-night in order to state the changes it is proposed to make in the regulations. In the budget speech I announced that a new schedule for the writing off of preproduction expenses on a forty per cent, thirty per cent, twenty per cent and ten per cent basis would be introduced. At the time of
the announcement our intention was that this new schedule would apply to the income of 1943 and thereafter. It has since been decided that this new schedule may be taken as applicable to 1942. The same provision will apply to the increase in the depreciation rate from fifteen per cent to twenty-five per cent.
A second concession related to the depletion allowance which would apply to those receiving royalty payments from wells spudded in during the period January 1, 1943, to March 31, 1945. The ordinary depletion rate in these cases was to be increased from twenty per cent to thirty-three and one-third per cent. Since the budget I have received further representations on this point, and I wish now to announce that the increase from twenty per cent to thirty-three and one-third per cent will be general in its application regardless of when the royalty well was brought into production. In respect of new royalty wells spudded in during the period January 1, 1943, to March 31, 1945, it is proposed to offer an additional concession. In these cases the trustee will be allowed to elect on behalf of the royalty holders to have the thirty-three and one-third per cent depletion rate apply indefinitely, as at present, or it may elect to receive a depletion rate of 100 per cent until disbursements by the trustee to the royalty holders equal the amount of subscribed capital, on the condition that after capital has been returned to the unit holders tax-free there shall subsequently be no depletion allowed.
Members who are interested in these concessions may want to read this in Hansard and give it a little thought. Apart from the amendment to resolution 17 which relates only to gas, these are the only changes which we propose to make in the oil resolutions. I shall deal with them later.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Questions have been asked as to how the government intends to improve the yield of oil in Canada at the present time. I may say that the oil controller, who was confronted with this problem by myself, appointed a committee of experienced producers with headquarters at Calgary. This committee was made up of small operators and representatives of the large oil companies. The committee met and formulated a number of recommendations which have been adopted by the government almost in toto. After he learned what the taxation proposals were, I heard a member of the committee state that in no part of the United States were more liberal tax concessions made to the oil industry than were being offered by this government. The purpose of our tax concessions was, of course,

The problem of obtaining oil to-day, particularly in Alberta, where the demands have been tremendously increased by activities on the Alaska highway, makes it imperative that Canada produce this year every barrel of oil that can be produced. We were advised that these tax changes would result in a very considerable increase in drilling by the owners of oil leases, and it is clearly evident at the moment that that is exactly what will take place. Two or three companies have bought new oil rigs, and the old and new rigs are being spudded-in. There will be a good deal of activity in such proven areas as we have. The intention is to drill out all remaining sites in Turner valley during the present summer. Those that will be drilled by the owners will, of course, be taken care of privately. The remainder in the field, and particularly properties on the flank of Turner valley, which is semi-proven territory will be drilled either by the owner; or if the owner is unable or unwilling to finance the development, the lease will be taken over by a crown company, which has recently been formed. The crown company will become the owner of the lease and will undertake the drilling of the well. After the well has been paid for, including the drilling costs and all other expenses incurred by the crown company, the well will be turned back to its former owner, for such further returns as the well may produce. That is the object of the crown company. I wish to emphasize that it is not the purpose of the crown company to wildcat for oil. The crown company is formed wholly to develop a certain proven or semi-proven area, and quickly obtain the maximum production from that area.
Is the crown company prepared to advance money to private owners who wish to borrow money to enable them to develop properties?

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: No. The purpose of the company is exactly what I have said, and it has no other authority. It is to drill out a particular area under a particular plan. To set up a government company which would provide money for anyone who wished to drill in wildcat areas would, of course, call for unlimited funds, and the likelihood of obtaining returns would be exceedingly small.
Has the government any facilities through which such moneys might be advanced?

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
No. Prior to the recent activity the government did enter into the oil business in a small way. The Vermilion area

was a proven area. Quite a number of wells had been drilled there by private enterprise. Everything about that field was known. It was known that a well in the proven area would return just about the cost of drilling or perhaps a little more. It was not a situation that invited the larger oil companies, and the private interests there were operating in a very limited way. It was not a large pool of oil; but it was sufficient, if drilled out completely, to take care of the requirements of the Canadian National Railways in that area for a considerable period.
In the Vermilion area?

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes. We tried to interest private capital. A number of companies looked the field over, and all decided that they would not go ahead. Nevertheless we felt that, even at some risk, the Canadian National Railways, having oil on its line, should itself undertake to provide itself with the oil required for its engines. The result was that the Canadian National Railways formed a subsidiary company, acquired leases in that area, and are drilling in that area for their own requirements. Whether the leases will pay out in full, so that the cost of the oil to the railway will not increase, is a matter that time will tell. In any event, the railway will obtain oil probably at about the normal price, and we shall be relieved of supplying at least that quantity of oil.

A good deal has been said about the royalty companies. The lack of interest in royalty companies has been attributed to the government's taxation. I suggest that the lack of interest in royalty companies is due to the record of the royalty companies. They are peculiar to Alberta, and peculiarly to Turner valley. The royalty companies were started, I think, in 1939. The record of the first royalty companies in 1941 was very good indeed. The drilling was all carried on in proven areas, and the yield of the royalty wells was above normal, so that a good market was created for royalty companies. But beginning with December, 1941, the record of royalty companies is really appalling. At the north end of Turner valley fifteen wells have been drilled, of which fourteen, or all but one, were royalty company wells. The record of those fifteen wells is that thirteen have * been abandoned) and two are still drilling. That is a tragedy, of course, for the investors in those royalty companies, but more than that it is a tragedy that fifteen wells had to be put down to prove a situation that could have been amply proved by two or three or, at the most, four wells. In other words, the fifteen wells proved that the drilling was in a barren area., and that is a very expensive way to prove that fact.
What is a royalty company? I wonder whether hon. members know just what the public is asked to participate in when they are asked to buy shares in a royalty company. The practice is that the owner of an oil lease, or a man who acquires an oil lease, puts in his lease and obtains for it twenty-five per cent of the gross ownership of the company. In other words, he is entitled to twenty-five per cent as gross royalties, and out of that he pays the royalty and provincial government dues.

It is not
essential at all that the lessor be reserved twenty-five per cent gross royalty.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
That is the standard situation to-day. It has been standardized. In the early days there were a number of ways of setting up the royalty company, but to-day twenty-five per cent is reserved as gross royalties, fifty-two per cent for preferred royalties, and twenty-three per cent as deferred royalties. That was worked out at various meetings of operators, brokers and security commissioners, held about a year ago.

The twenty-five per cent royalty to the promoter is on gross production, before any deductions are made for productive operations. These twenty-five per cent gross royalties are allowed the promoter, out of which landowner's and provincial royalty is paid. The fifty-two per cent of preferred royalty is the money raised from the public to drill the well. Fifty-two per cent of the well is sold to the public. Out of that, on the usual basis, the return for one per cent ownership of the well is generally S3.500, but a commission of twenty-five per cent is allowed the broker who sells those shares, so that the $3,500 paid in to the company for actual drilling actually costs the public $4,375. That is the shrinkage before the money ever gets to the well. In other words, the public subscribes $227,500 for drilling, of which $182,000 only is net to the company. Then a drilling contract is let, usually for a certain number of feet of drilling. We will say that the company is successful in finding oil. If it is successful, the twenty-five per cent royalty to the promoter is from the gross; fifty-two per cent goes to pay off the preferred royalties-in other words, it is a return of the money to the investor-and the last twenty-three per cent is divided half to the investor and half to the promoter, after the preferred has been retired in full.
That may or may not be a fair basis in which to invite the public to participate. Personally I do not think the public get a very good run for their money, although I will say that in the early days the public did well from royalty companies. As each well came in-they were drilling in proven territory-the public did get the return of their money plus quite substantial dividends. However, to use that type of financing for wildcatting is, of course, hopeless. The hon. member who spoke last referred to it as "wild" money. I have heard it referred to as "mad" money. It is contended to-night that it is necessary to have that kind of money in order to bring in wells in wildcat territory. I doubt that very much. If anyone cares to defend that type of financing of oil wells in wildcat territory, I must take an opposite view.
May I ask the minister how he would propose to wildcat to discover new areas-by what means? Would he put the government into it?

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
No. But I think the hon. member will find that there will be more wildcatting this year and in the succeeding years. In fact, more wildcatting is being done at this moment in Canada than there has been for

a number of years; and under the basis of taxation proposed there will be more wildcatting carried on. A well-financed syndicate can afford to wildcat, on the theory that eventually they will hit paying wells. They are able to accumulate the costs of their wildcat-ting until they do prove up an area, and can then recover the costs which have been previously incurred.
I hope, therefore, there will be no further suggestions that the taxation proposed is killing the royalty business. Nothing could be farther from the truth. It is the record of the royalty business itself which has killed that type of financing.
